title: Performance

techniques.name: AST-Precise Localization
techniques.q: Exactly which lines need to change?
techniques.what: Instead of reading whole files or grepping text, the agent parses code into an abstract syntax tree and navigates by structure: the function, its callers, the class it belongs to. It loads and edits only the nodes involved, which saves context, avoids broken edits and speeds up finding the fault.
use: Coding agents working in large repositories
Bug fixes that start from a stack trace or failing test
Refactors that must touch every caller of a function
metrics: signatures of classes and functions, not full bodies
file → class or function → lines (as in Agentless)
replace a node, then re-parse to validate
steps: Build a repo map of symbols and signatures with tree-sitter
Localize top-down: candidate files, then functions, then line ranges
Load only the selected nodes plus their immediate context
Validate every edit by re-parsing and running the tests
pitfalls: Dynamic code (reflection, metaprogramming) hides real call paths
Parsers lag behind new language syntax
Too narrow a view misses side effects in other files
techniques.remember: Navigate by structure, edit by node.
techniques.cap: Token counts are illustrative. The saving grows with file size.

techniques.name: Speculative Decoding
techniques.q: Can a small model draft tokens for the big one?
techniques.what: A fast draft model proposes several tokens ahead. The large target model checks them all in a single forward pass and keeps the longest correct prefix, supplying its own token at the first mismatch. With the standard acceptance rule the output matches what the target model would have produced alone. Reported speed-ups are typically around 2–3×.
use: Interactive products where tokens per second matters
Long outputs such as code, reports and documents
Edits that copy large parts of the input (prompt lookup)
metrics: a small model, or extra heads (Medusa, EAGLE)
the target scores all drafted tokens in parallel
draft by copying n-grams from the prompt
steps: Pick a draft that shares the target’s tokenizer
Measure acceptance rate on your real prompts
Tune lookahead k; too high wastes verification work
Use prompt-lookup decoding for code edits that repeat the input
pitfalls: A low acceptance rate gives little or even negative speed-up
The draft model needs extra GPU memory
Gains shrink at large batch sizes, when the GPU is already busy
techniques.remember: Draft fast, verify in one pass.
techniques.cap: Accepted tokens are free extra output. The first mismatch is replaced by the target’s own token.

techniques.name: Prefix Caching
techniques.q: Why recompute the same prompt start?
techniques.what: Inside the inference server, the key–value (KV) cache for a prompt prefix is kept after a request finishes and reused by the next request that starts with the same tokens. The shared part skips prefill entirely, cutting time to first token for agents that resend the same system prompt, tools and history at every step. It is the engine-level mechanism behind provider prompt caching.
use: Self-hosted models serving agents with long, repeated prompts
Many users sharing one system prompt
Multi-turn chats where each turn extends the last
metrics: attention keys and values for tokens already processed
KV cache stored in blocks that requests can share (vLLM)
a prefix tree of cached blocks (SGLang)
send requests to the replica that holds their prefix
steps: Turn on automatic prefix caching in your serving engine
Keep the prompt prefix stable across turns and users
Route sessions to the same replica to keep caches warm
Track cache hit rate and time to first token
pitfalls: Any change early in the prompt forces a full recompute
Cached blocks compete with live requests for GPU memory
Across many replicas, hit rate falls without cache-aware routing
techniques.cap: Only the few hundred new tokens per user need prefill. The shared 6,000 are reused.

cmp.needs: Time to first token, GPU cost

techniques.name: Disaggregated Prefill
techniques.q: Why make prefill and decode share a GPU?
techniques.what: Inference has two phases with different needs. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and is compute-bound; decode produces one token at a time and is limited by memory bandwidth. Running them on separate GPU pools and handing the KV cache across stops long prompts from stalling other users’ token streams, and lets each pool be sized and tuned on its own.
use: High-traffic serving with long prompts and many concurrent streams
Strict targets for both time to first token and tokens per second
Large deployments where GPU utilization matters
metrics: compute-bound; sets time to first token (TTFT)
memory-bound; sets time per output token (TPOT)
cache moved from prefill to decode workers over fast links
tune the prefill-to-decode GPU ratio to traffic
steps: Measure TTFT and TPOT separately under real load
Consider disaggregation when long prompts and many streams compete
Use a fast interconnect (NVLink, RDMA) for KV transfer
Rebalance the prefill-to-decode ratio as traffic shifts
pitfalls: KV transfer adds network overhead and complexity
Little benefit for small models or light traffic
More components to operate and monitor
techniques.remember: Compute-heavy prefill, memory-heavy decode: split them.
techniques.cap: On a shared GPU the long prefill blocks decoding. Separate pools keep tokens flowing.

techniques.name: Agent Execution Graphs
techniques.q: Which steps can run at the same time?
techniques.what: Model the agent’s work as a directed acyclic graph of steps with explicit dependencies, instead of a strictly sequential loop. Independent tool calls and sub-agents run in parallel, results join where needed, and the runtime can checkpoint, retry a failed node, or resume without redoing the rest.
use: Tasks with several independent lookups or tool calls
Multi-agent systems with sub-agents working side by side
Long workflows that must survive failures and restarts
metrics: steps and the data they depend on
merge results before the next step
the longest chain sets total latency
resume from the last completed node
steps: Map the task’s steps and what each one needs as input
Run independent tool calls in parallel (parallel tool use or async)
Give every node a timeout and a retry policy
Measure the critical path and shorten that first
pitfalls: Hidden dependencies cause race conditions
Parallel calls can hit rate limits all at once
Static graphs are rigid, so allow dynamic planning where needed
techniques.remember: Parallel where independent, join where needed.
techniques.cap: Total time is set by the critical path: A, then the slowest of B, C and D, then E.

techniques.name: Latency Budgets and Streaming
techniques.q: Where do the seconds go before users see anything?
techniques.what: Set a user-facing budget for the whole request, such as first words within 3 s and the full answer within 5.5 s at p95, then measure p50 and p95 for every stage and change the shape of the request until it fits. The main levers sit in your application, not the model server: stream status and tokens, run independent calls in parallel, cut sequential LLM hops, use a faster model for early steps, and put a timeout with a planned fallback on each slow dependency. Serving-level speed-ups such as prefix caching and speculative decoding shorten individual stages; this technique decides which stages to shorten and what the user sees while they run.
use: Chat and support assistants where users leave if the screen stays blank
Agents that chain several LLM calls, tools and retrieval before answering
Launch reviews where a product owner asks for a latency target in writing
metrics: targets for first visible text, first answer words and total time, set at p95
p50 and p95 per stage: each LLM call, tool and retrieval
the chain of waits that sets the total; only shortening it helps
a status line early, then answer tokens as they are generated
each sequential model call adds its own first-token and generation time
a cap on each slow dependency and a planned, labelled degraded answer
steps: Write the budget as p95 targets for first words and total time
Trace every stage and record p50 and p95, not averages
Remove waits: parallel independent calls, merge or shrink LLM hops, stream early
Cap slow dependencies with timeouts and count the answers that fall back
pitfalls: Budgeting on p50 alone: the slow 5% is where users leave
A timeout so tight that a fifth of answers quietly degrade
Streaming a blank-looking wait, such as a spinner with no status, and calling it solved
techniques.remember: Budget the p95, not the average. Show something early, wait on less.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Tejas Trade, a fictional stockbroking app, answering “why did my order fail?”.

techniques.name: Serving Engines and Continuous Batching
techniques.q: How many requests can one GPU serve, and at what cost?
techniques.what: When you run open-weight models yourself, the serving engine decides how much work each GPU does. A naive server generates one request at a time and leaves the GPU mostly idle. Static batching waits for a batch to fill and for its longest answer to finish. Engines such as vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and TGI use continuous batching, which adds a new request to the running batch at every decoding step, and paged KV-cache memory (PagedAttention), which packs many more sequences into GPU memory. The result is several times more tokens per second per GPU and a lower cost per million tokens. Capacity is then sized from load and a latency target. Prefix caching, speculative decoding and disaggregated prefill are separate techniques in this module that these engines also implement.
use: Self-hosting open models for cost, data residency or latency
Serving a fine-tuned or distilled small model
High-volume internal workloads such as classification or extraction
metrics: requests join and leave the running batch at every step
PagedAttention allocates the cache in pages; memory, not compute, often limits batch size
output tokens per second per GPU at your prompt and answer lengths
time to first token and p95 end-to-end at your load
load divided by capacity; above about 80% queues and latency grow fast
GPU price per hour ÷ millions of tokens served per hour
steps: Measure prompt and answer lengths and the peak requests per second
Serve with a continuous-batching engine and load-test at realistic traffic
Tune max sequences, memory use and context length; add GPUs or replicas for the latency target
Compare cost per million tokens and p95 with a hosted API before committing
pitfalls: Benchmarking with one request at a time and concluding the GPU is slow
Running near 100% utilisation, where p95 latency explodes
Setting a very long max context that reserves KV memory and shrinks the batch
techniques.remember: Continuous batching plus paged KV memory; size GPUs for p95 at peak.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Bharat Bol, a fictional voice-bot company, self-hosts an 8B model for Hindi support calls.

techniques.name: Quantisation for Inference (FP8, INT4, KV Cache)
techniques.q: Can a big model run on fewer GPUs without losing quality?
techniques.what: Quantisation stores a model’s weights, and sometimes its activations and KV cache, in fewer bits so it needs less GPU memory and moves less data per token. FP8 (weights and activations) roughly halves memory versus BF16 with very little quality loss on recent GPUs. Weight-only 4-bit methods such as AWQ and GPTQ cut memory about 4× and suit small-batch or single-GPU serving, with a larger quality drop, especially on small models. An FP8 KV cache frees memory for more concurrent sequences. The gains show up as fewer GPUs, higher throughput and lower cost per token, but quality must be measured on your own tasks, including Indian languages and long context. Compressing embedding vectors is a separate technique in module 5.
use: Fitting a 70B-class model on one or two GPUs
Cutting cost per token for self-hosted models
Running models on laptops and edge devices (GGUF)
metrics: 8-bit weights and activations; Hopper-class GPUs and newer; usually within a fraction of a point
AWQ, GPTQ; about 0.5 byte per parameter plus overhead; bigger loss on small models
FP8 KV halves cache memory, so more sequences fit
a few hundred representative prompts to set scales
your own task scores, per language and context length, before and after
steps: Measure baseline quality, throughput and memory in BF16
Quantise with calibration data from your own traffic (FP8 first)
Serve with the quantised weights and, if needed, an FP8 KV cache
Re-run your evals per language and length; roll back if the loss exceeds your limit
pitfalls: Calibrating on English web text for a Hindi and Tamil workload
Judging quality on a general benchmark instead of your tasks
Assuming 4-bit is always faster; at large batch it can be slower than FP8
techniques.remember: Fewer bits, fewer GPUs; FP8 first, and measure on your own tasks.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Nyaya Sahayak, a fictional legal-research service, self-hosts a 70B model on 80 GB GPUs.

LOG = []                                                     #@1
def record(task, steps, tests_passed):                       #@1
    if tests_passed:                  # keep only verified runs  #@1
        LOG.append({"kind": task.kind, "steps": steps})      #@1

def distill(kind, min_runs=3):                               #@2
    runs = [r for r in LOG if r["kind"] == kind]             #@2
    if len(runs) < min_runs:                                 #@2
        return None                                          #@2
    best = min(runs, key=lambda r: len(r["steps"]))          #@2
    return Skill(name=kind, steps=best["steps"], check="make test")   #@2

skill = distill("add_api_endpoint")                          #@2,3
store.add(text=skill.description, item=skill,                #@3
          meta={"commit": git_head(), "failures": 0})        #@3

hit = store.search(new_task.text, k=1)[0]                    #@4
if hit.score >= 0.80:                                        #@4
    plan = hit.item.steps                  # reuse the skill #@4
else:
    plan = agent.explore(new_task)         # no match: explore   #@4

agent.follow(plan)                                           #@5
if run(skill.check) != 0:                  # verify every reuse  #@5,6
    hit.meta["failures"] += 1                                #@6
    if hit.meta["failures"] >= 2:                            #@6
        store.retire(skill.name)           # stale after a refactor  #@6
steps: Log verified runs
Record each successful trajectory with the kind of task it solved. Only runs whose tests passed are kept, so mistakes are not memorized.
Distill a repeated routine
After three runs of the same kind, keep the shortest one as a named skill: four steps plus a check (make test) that proves it worked.
Index the skill
Store the skill under its description, with the commit it was learned on and a failure counter, so it can be found and audited later.
Retrieve at the start of a task
A new task, adding a /payouts endpoint, matches the skill with similarity 0.86, above the 0.80 threshold, so the agent loads the skill instead of exploring.
Follow it and verify
The agent finishes in 4 steps instead of 9 and runs the skill’s check. Verification is what makes reuse safe.
Revise or retire
After a refactor the skill fails its check twice, so it is retired and the next run explores and learns a fresh version.

import tree_sitter_python as tspython
from tree_sitter import Language, Parser
parser = Parser(Language(tspython.language()))                     #@1

def symbols(path):                                                 #@1
    tree = parser.parse(open(path, "rb").read())                   #@1
    for node in walk(tree.root_node):                              #@1
        if node.type in ("class_definition", "function_definition"):   #@1
            name = node.child_by_field_name("name").text.decode()  #@1
            yield path, name, node.start_point[0] + 1              #@1

repo_map = [s for p in python_files("app/") for s in symbols(p)]   #@1
issue = "Tax is wrong on invoices above INR 1 lakh"
files = llm_rank(issue, sorted({p for p, _, _ in repo_map}))[:3]   #@2
funcs = llm_rank(issue, [s for s in repo_map if s[0] in files])[:1]   #@3
path, name, _ = funcs[0]                                           #@3
node = find_function(parser.parse(read(path)).root_node, name)     #@3
callers = find_references(path, name)       # LSP or ast-grep      #@4
context = [node.text.decode()] + [c.text for c in callers]         #@4

patch = llm_edit(issue, context)                                   #@5
src = read(path)
new_src = src[:node.start_byte] + patch + src[node.end_byte:]      #@5
assert not parser.parse(new_src).root_node.has_error   # re-parse  #@5
write(path, new_src)                                               #@5,6
assert run("pytest tests/test_billing.py") == 0                    #@6
steps: Build a repo map
Parse every file with tree-sitter and keep only class and function names with their line numbers: 340 files become about 4,100 symbols.
Localize the file
Given the issue text, the model ranks files from the map, not from full source. billing.py comes first.
Narrow to the function
Inside billing.py it picks Invoice.apply_tax. The syntax tree gives its exact span: lines 42 to 57.
Add the immediate context
Find-references returns two callers, one in export.py. Function plus callers is 56 lines, about 560 tokens, against 30,000 for the whole file.
Edit the node, then re-parse
The patch replaces only that function’s bytes. Re-parsing confirms the file still has no syntax errors before anything is saved.
Run the tests
The billing tests pass. The change touched 15 lines, and a reviewer can read the whole diff in a minute.

def speculative_step(tokens, k=4):
    draft = []                                                 #@1
    for _ in range(k):                                         #@1
        draft.append(small.greedy_next(tokens + draft))        #@1
    preds = big.greedy_all(tokens + draft)   # 1 pass, k+1 predictions   #@2
    out = []
    for i, tok in enumerate(draft):                            #@3
        if tok != preds[i]:                                    #@3,4
            out.append(preds[i])        # target's own token   #@4
            return out, i                                      #@4
        out.append(tok)                 # accepted             #@3
    out.append(preds[k])                # all k accepted: bonus token   #@3
    return out, k

accepted = checked = 0                                         #@5
while not finished(tokens):
    new, acc = speculative_step(tokens)                        #@5
    tokens += new                                              #@5
    accepted += acc                                            #@5
    checked += acc + (1 if acc < 4 else 0)                     #@5
alpha = accepted / checked            # per-token acceptance   #@5,6

c = 0.05                              # draft cost ÷ target pass   #@6
tokens_per_pass = (1 - alpha ** 5) / (1 - alpha)               #@6
speedup = tokens_per_pass / (1 + 4 * c)                        #@6
steps: Draft k tokens cheaply
The small draft model proposes k = 4 tokens one after another. Each draft step costs a small fraction of a target pass.
Verify all of them in one pass
The target model runs once over the prompt plus the 4 drafts and produces its own prediction at every position, 5 in total.
Accept the longest matching prefix
“five” and “business” match the target’s predictions, so both are kept. This sketch uses greedy matching; with sampling, a probabilistic rule keeps the target’s distribution exactly.
Replace the first mismatch
The target wanted “days”, not “weeks”. Its token is used and the rest of the draft is discarded: 3 new tokens from one target pass.
Measure acceptance
Count accepted drafts against drafts checked. Over this run the per-token acceptance rate α is 0.70; on real prompts it is the number that decides everything.
Estimate the speed-up
With k = 4 and α = 0.7, a pass yields (1 − 0.7⁵) ÷ 0.3 ≈ 2.77 tokens. Dividing by the cost 1 + 4 × 0.05 = 1.2 gives about 2.3×.

from collections import OrderedDict
BLOCK = 16                                    # tokens per KV block   #@1
cache = OrderedDict()                         # block hash -> KV block on GPU   #@3

def block_hashes(tokens):                                            #@1,2
    h, out = None, []                                                #@2
    for i in range(0, len(tokens) - len(tokens) % BLOCK, BLOCK):     #@1
        h = hash((h, tuple(tokens[i:i + BLOCK])))   # chained with parent   #@2
        out.append(h)                                                #@2
    return out

def prefill(tokens):
    hashes = block_hashes(tokens)
    hit = 0
    while hit < len(hashes) and hashes[hit] in cache:                #@4,5
        cache.move_to_end(hashes[hit])            # recently used    #@4,6
        hit += 1                                                     #@4
    reused = [cache[h] for h in hashes[:hit]]                        #@4
    fresh = model.compute_kv(tokens[hit * BLOCK:], past=reused)      #@3,4
    for h, kv in zip(hashes[hit:], fresh):                           #@3
        cache[h] = kv                                                #@3
    while gpu_blocks_used() > LIMIT:                                 #@6
        cache.popitem(last=False)                 # evict least recently used   #@6
    return reused + fresh, hit * BLOCK            # tokens skipped   #@4,6
steps: Cut the prompt into blocks
The KV cache is stored in fixed blocks, 16 tokens each in vLLM. The 6,000-token system prompt and tools fill 375 blocks.
Hash each block with its parent
Each block’s key includes the hash of everything before it, so a block can only match when the whole prefix up to it is identical.
First request: a miss
Nothing is cached yet, so all 6,300 tokens are prefilled: 0.63 s at 10,000 tokens per second. The blocks are kept afterwards.
Next request: reuse the prefix
User B’s prompt shares the first 375 blocks. They are looked up, not recomputed, and only 300 new tokens are prefilled: 0.03 s.
One early change breaks the chain
Put a timestamp in the first line and the first block differs, so every later hash differs too. The whole prompt is recomputed.
Evict cold blocks, watch the hit rate
When GPU memory is needed, the least recently used blocks are evicted. Track cache hit rate and time to first token together.

# 1. Measure the two phases separately, from serving logs
ttft = [r.first_token_at - r.arrived_at for r in reqs]              #@1
tpot = [(r.done_at - r.first_token_at) / (r.out_tokens - 1) for r in reqs]   #@1
print(p95(ttft), p95(tpot))        # shared GPUs: 2.2 s, 61 ms       #@1

stall = 1.5 / 0.030                # 30k-token prefill ÷ 30 ms per token = 50   #@2

PREFILL = Pool(gpus=2, role="prefill")     # compute-bound work     #@3
DECODE  = Pool(gpus=6, role="decode")      # memory-bandwidth-bound  #@3

async def serve(req):
    p = PREFILL.least_loaded()                                       #@3
    kv, first = await p.prefill(req.prompt)                          #@3
    d = DECODE.least_loaded()                                        #@4
    await d.receive_kv(kv, link="rdma")    # 30k × 128 KiB ≈ 3.9 GB  #@4
    yield first                                                      #@5
    async for tok in d.decode(kv, max_tokens=req.max_tokens):        #@5
        yield tok                          # no prefill in this pool #@5

def rebalance():                                                     #@6
    if p95(ttft) > TTFT_SLO and p95(tpot) < TPOT_SLO:                #@6
        move_gpu(src=DECODE, dst=PREFILL)                            #@6
    elif p95(tpot) > TPOT_SLO and p95(ttft) < TTFT_SLO:              #@6
        move_gpu(src=PREFILL, dst=DECODE)                            #@6
steps: Measure TTFT and TPOT separately
Averages hide the problem. On shared GPUs, p95 time to first token is 2.2 s and p95 time per output token is 61 ms, above a 50 ms target.
See the interference
A 30,000-token prefill occupies a GPU for about 1.5 s. Every stream decoding on that GPU waits: 1.5 s ÷ 30 ms = 50 tokens it could have produced.
Split into two pools
Prefill runs on its own GPUs, which are compute-bound. Decode runs on the others, which are limited by memory bandwidth. Here 2 and 6 of 8 GPUs.
Hand over the KV cache
The finished prompt’s KV cache moves to a decode GPU. For an 8B model with 8 KV heads that is 128 KiB per token, about 3.9 GB, roughly 80 ms over 400 Gb/s RDMA.
Decode stays steady
No prefill ever lands in the decode pool, so p95 TPOT falls to about 35 ms while the long prompts are still processed.
Rebalance as traffic shifts
If TTFT breaches its target while TPOT has room, move a GPU to prefill; if TPOT breaches, move one back to decode.

import asyncio

DEPS = {"A": [], "B": ["A"], "C": ["A"], "D": ["A"],             #@1
        "E": ["B", "C", "D"]}                                     #@1
SECS = {"A": 1, "B": 3, "C": 2, "D": 4, "E": 1}                   #@1,6
limit = asyncio.Semaphore(3)        # cap concurrent calls         #@3
done = {}                           # checkpoint of finished nodes #@4

async def run(name):
    for attempt in range(3):                                      #@4
        try:
            async with limit:                                     #@3
                return await asyncio.wait_for(TOOLS[name](done), timeout=10)   #@4
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:                              #@4
            await asyncio.sleep(2 ** attempt)    # back off, retry #@4
    raise RuntimeError(f"{name} failed 3 times")

async def execute():
    pending = {n: d for n, d in DEPS.items() if n not in done}    #@2,4
    while pending:
        ready = [n for n, d in pending.items() if all(x in done for x in d)]   #@2
        results = await asyncio.gather(*(run(n) for n in ready))  #@3,5
        for n, r in zip(ready, results):                          #@5
            done[n] = r                                           #@5
            del pending[n]                                        #@5

def finish(n):                      # earliest finish time of n   #@6
    return SECS[n] + max((finish(d) for d in DEPS[n]), default=0)   #@6
print(finish("E"), sum(SECS.values()))    # 6 vs 11 seconds       #@6
steps: Declare steps and dependencies
Write the work as a graph: A fetches the application; B, C and D each need only A; E needs all three. Durations are 1, 3, 2, 4 and 1 s.
Find what is ready
A node is ready when everything it depends on is done. After A finishes, B, C and D are all ready at once.
Fan out, with a cap
Start every ready node together. A semaphore caps concurrent calls so a wide fan-out does not trip rate limits.
Time out, retry, checkpoint
Each node has a timeout and retries with backoff. Finished nodes are checkpointed, so a restart resumes instead of redoing them.
Join before the next step
E starts only when B, C and D have all returned, and it receives all three results.
Find the critical path
Total time is set by the longest chain: A, D, E = 1 + 4 + 1 = 6 s, against 11 s in sequence. Only speeding up D would help further.

import asyncio, time
from statistics import quantiles

BUDGET = {"first_words_p95": 3.0, "total_p95": 5.5}   # seconds, per request   #@1
SPANS = {}                                                                  #@2

class span:                                  # time one stage of the request   #@2
    def __init__(self, stage): self.stage = stage
    def __enter__(self): self.t0 = time.perf_counter()
    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        SPANS.setdefault(self.stage, []).append(time.perf_counter() - self.t0)  #@2

def p95(stage):                                                             #@2
    return quantiles(SPANS[stage], n=20)[-1]      # the 95th percentile      #@2

async def exchange_log(order_id):
    try:
        return await asyncio.wait_for(fetch_exchange_log(order_id), timeout=1.5)  #@5
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:                                            #@5
        return {"reason": None, "degraded": True}   # answer from the rest    #@5

async def why_failed(order_id, question, send):
    await send({"type": "status", "text": "Checking your order…"})   # ~0.3 s  #@3
    with span("tools"):
        status, margin, log = await asyncio.gather(                         #@4
            order_status(order_id), margin_check(order_id),                  #@4
            exchange_log(order_id))                                          #@4,5
    with span("retrieval"):
        docs = await search_help(log["reason"] or status["code"])  # needs a code  #@4
    prompt = build_prompt(question, status, margin, log, docs)  # no intent call  #@6
    with span("answer"):
        async for text in llm_stream(prompt):          # one hop, streamed     #@3,6
            await send({"type": "token", "text": text})                     #@3
    return log.get("degraded", False)                  # count fallbacks      #@5
steps: Write the budget down

Tejas Trade, a fictional stockbroking app, sets two p95 targets for “why did my order fail?”: the first words of the answer within 3.0 s and the whole answer within 5.5 s. p95 means 95 of every 100 users get at least this; averages hide the slow ones who leave.
Measure every stage

Wrap each stage in a span and keep p50 and p95. The first trace: intent call 600 / 900 ms, three tools in turn 1,550 / 3,400 ms, retrieval 150 / 200 ms, answer call 2,400 / 3,200 ms. Total 4,700 ms at p50 and 7,700 ms at p95, with a blank screen throughout.
Show something early

A status line goes out at once, about 0.3 s after the tap, and the answer streams token by token. The user now sees words when the first token arrives, 500 ms into the answer call, instead of after all 2,400 ms.
Wait on less: run tools together

Order status (300 ms), margin check (450 ms) and the exchange rejection log (800 ms) do not need each other, so gather runs them at once: 800 ms at p50 instead of 1,550. Retrieval needs the rejection code, so it still waits.
Cap the slow tool

The exchange log has a long tail: p95 2,400 ms. A 1.5 s timeout caps it; the 8% of calls that run over get an answer built from order status and margin, and the function returns a flag so fallbacks are counted, not hidden.
Cut an LLM hop

The separate intent call (600 / 900 ms) is gone: the app already knows the question type from the button, so the answer call reads the question itself. The longer prompt adds about 100 ms. First words at p95: 1.5 + 0.2 + 0.9 = 2.6 s; total p95: 1.5 + 0.2 + 3.3 = 5.0 s. Both budgets are met.

# shell: vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B --max-num-seqs 128 \                         #@1,2
#        --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --max-model-len 8192                     #@3
import asyncio, time
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url="http://gpu-1:8000/v1", api_key="local")

async def one(prompt):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    r = await client.chat.completions.create(model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B", max_tokens=300,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return time.perf_counter() - t, r.usage.completion_tokens

async def load(rps, seconds=120):                                              #@4
    tasks = []
    for _ in range(rps * seconds):
        tasks.append(asyncio.create_task(one(sample_prompt())))
        await asyncio.sleep(1 / rps)
    res = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    lat = sorted(r[0] for r in res)
    return lat[int(len(lat) * 0.95)], sum(r[1] for r in res) / seconds     #@4,5

p95, tok_s = asyncio.run(load(rps=8))
print(f"p95 {p95:.1f}s  {tok_s:.0f} tok/s  ₹/1M = {2 * 220 / (tok_s * 3600 / 1e6):.0f}")  #@6
steps: Start a continuous-batching server
Bharat Bol, a fictional voice-bot company, serves an 8B model with vLLM. The server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so the app code does not change.
Let the batch grow
max-num-seqs lets up to 128 sequences share the GPU. New requests join the running batch at each step instead of waiting for a batch to finish.
Leave room for the KV cache
90% of GPU memory is given to weights and the paged KV cache. A shorter max context of 8,192 tokens leaves room for more sequences.
Load-test at real traffic
Replay 8 requests a second of real prompts for two minutes. One-at-a-time tests make any GPU look slow.
Read p95 and throughput
One GPU serves the 2,400 tokens a second but runs 80% busy, so p95 is 18 s. Two GPUs bring p95 to 8 s.
Compare the cost
At ₹220 per GPU-hour, two GPUs cost about ₹51 per million output tokens. Compare that, and p95, with a hosted API before committing.

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from llmcompressor import oneshot
from llmcompressor.modifiers.quantization import QuantizationModifier

MODEL = "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct"                                 #@1
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL, torch_dtype="auto")
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL)

recipe = QuantizationModifier(targets="Linear", scheme="FP8_DYNAMIC",       #@2
                              ignore=["lm_head"])
oneshot(model=model, recipe=recipe)                                         #@2
model.save_pretrained("llama70b-fp8"); tok.save_pretrained("llama70b-fp8")

# shell: vllm serve ./llama70b-fp8 --tensor-parallel-size 2 \               #@3
#        --kv-cache-dtype fp8                                               #@4
# eval: lm_eval --model local-chat-completions --tasks our_legal_qa_hi_en   #@5
# BF16 86.0 → FP8 85.5; GPUs 4 → 2; ₹208 → ₹95 per 1M tokens               #@6
steps: Start from a baseline
Nyaya Sahayak, a fictional legal-research service, runs a 70B model. In BF16 its 140 GB of weights plus KV cache need four 80 GB GPUs.
Quantise to FP8
FP8 dynamic quantisation needs no calibration set: weights are converted once and activations are scaled on the fly. The weights shrink to about 70 GB.
Serve on fewer GPUs
The FP8 model fits on two GPUs with tensor parallelism instead of four.
Quantise the KV cache
An FP8 KV cache halves cache memory, so more sequences fit and throughput rises.
Re-run your own evals
Score the legal Q&A set in Hindi and English, short and long context, before and after.
Decide on the numbers
Quality moves from 86.0 to 85.5, GPUs from 4 to 2 and cost from about ₹208 to ₹95 per million tokens. 4-bit would fit on one GPU but lose 1.5 points.

# Conceptual flow implemented by NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d or vLLM's disaggregated mode

async def handle(request):
    prefill = least_loaded(PREFILL_POOL)            # compute-heavy GPUs
    kv, first_token = await prefill.run(request.prompt)

    decode = least_loaded(DECODE_POOL)              # memory-bandwidth-heavy GPUs
    await decode.receive_kv(kv)                     # transfer over NVLink / RDMA
    yield first_token
    async for token in decode.generate(max_tokens=request.max_tokens):
        yield token

# Scale each pool from its own metric:
#   time to first token too high   -> add prefill workers
#   time per output token too high -> add decode workers

latbudget.sc: Tejas Trade, a fictional stockbroking app, has an assistant that answers “why did my order fail?”. The first version made an intent call, three tool calls one after another, a help-article search and an answer call, and showed a spinner for 4.7 s (7.7 s at p95). The team set a budget of first words within 3 s and the full answer within 5.5 s at p95, traced every stage, and then streamed a status line and tokens, ran the tools in parallel, dropped the intent call and put a 1.5 s timeout on the slow exchange log. The p95 total fell to 5.0 s and first words to 2.6 s, with 8% of answers built without the exchange’s reason.
latbudget.an: A restaurant kitchen at dinner rush. The waiter brings water and bread at once (the status line), the chef cooks the dal, rice and sabzi on three burners together (parallel calls), nobody takes the order twice (one LLM hop), and if the tandoor is backed up the table is offered a different bread rather than a forty-minute wait (timeout and fallback).
ind: Order, UPI and payout “what happened?” questions that must answer before the user retries or calls support
Bill and recharge assistants that stream a status line while plan and usage lookups run in parallel
Order-tracking chat where a slow courier API is capped by a timeout and answered from the last known scan
lib: AsyncAnthropic streams a message as it is generated; asyncio runs the tool calls in parallel and times out the slow one.
code:
import asyncio, time
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic()                     # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
MODEL = "claude-haiku-4-5"                    # example id: a fast model for this path

async def order_status(oid):  await asyncio.sleep(0.30); return {"code": "RMS_MARGIN", "state": "rejected"}
async def margin_check(oid):  await asyncio.sleep(0.45); return {"shortfall_inr": 1840}
async def exchange_log(oid):  await asyncio.sleep(0.80); return {"reason": "Insufficient margin at RMS"}
async def search_help(code):  await asyncio.sleep(0.15); return ["Why orders are rejected for margin"]

async def capped(coro, seconds, fallback):
    try:
        return await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout=seconds)
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        return fallback

async def why_failed(oid, question):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    print("[status] Checking your order…", flush=True)            # visible at once
    status, margin, log = await asyncio.gather(                   # parallel tools
        order_status(oid), margin_check(oid),
        capped(exchange_log(oid), 1.5, {"reason": None, "degraded": True}))
    docs = await search_help(log["reason"] or status["code"])     # needs the code
    prompt = (f"Question: {question}\nOrder: {status}\nMargin: {margin}\n"
              f"Exchange: {log}\nHelp: {docs}\n"
              "Explain in two sentences why the order failed and what to do. "
              "If the exchange reason is missing, say so.")
    first = None
    async with client.messages.stream(model=MODEL, max_tokens=300,
                                      messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]) as stream:
        async for text in stream.text_stream:                     # one hop, streamed
            if first is None:
                first = time.perf_counter() - t0
            print(text, end="", flush=True)
    total = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"\nfirst words {first:.2f} s · total {total:.2f} s · degraded {log.get('degraded', False)}")

asyncio.run(why_failed("ORD-5521", "Why did my order fail?"))
latbudget.note: The tool functions are stubs that sleep for their p50 times. The model id is an example; use one available to your account. The same pattern works with any provider that streams over server-sent events.

serving.sc: Bharat Bol, a fictional voice-bot company, self-hosts an 8B model for Hindi support calls because call transcripts must stay in its own cloud. Its first server generated one answer at a time and queued at 2 requests a second. With vLLM’s continuous batching and paged KV cache, one GPU handles 8 requests a second (2,400 output tokens a second) at 80% busy with a p95 of 18 s; two GPUs bring p95 to 8 s at about ₹51 per million output tokens.

import time
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B", gpu_memory_utilization=0.90, max_model_len=8192)
params = SamplingParams(max_tokens=300, temperature=0.2)

prompts = [f"Summarise this support call in Hindi, ticket {i}: ..." for i in range(512)]
t = time.perf_counter()
outs = llm.generate(prompts, params)
secs = time.perf_counter() - t

tokens = sum(len(o.outputs[0].token_ids) for o in outs)
print(f"{tokens / secs:.0f} output tokens/s across {len(prompts)} prompts")
serving.note: Needs a CUDA GPU with enough memory for the model. The offline API shown batches all prompts at once; for live traffic use vllm serve and a load test.

quant.sc: Nyaya Sahayak, a fictional legal-research service, self-hosts a 70B model so case files stay in its own cloud. In BF16 the model needs four 80 GB GPUs and costs about ₹208 per million tokens. It converts the weights to FP8, serves on two GPUs with an FP8 KV cache, and re-runs its Hindi and English legal Q&A evals: quality moves from 86.0 to 85.5 and cost falls to about ₹95 per million tokens. A 4-bit version would fit on one GPU but lose 1.5 points, so it is kept for a low-priority batch workload only.
quant.an: Saving photos as high-quality JPEGs instead of RAW files: a quarter of the space, and nobody can tell the difference at normal viewing size, but you still check the ones that matter.

from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

questions = [l.strip() for l in open("legal_qa_hi_en.txt", encoding="utf-8")][:200]
params = SamplingParams(max_tokens=256, temperature=0)

llm = LLM(model="RedHatAI/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-FP8-dynamic",
          tensor_parallel_size=2, kv_cache_dtype="fp8", max_model_len=8192)
outs = llm.generate(questions, params)

with open("answers_fp8.jsonl", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for q, o in zip(questions, outs):
        f.write(f'{{"q": {q!r}, "a": {o.outputs[0].text!r}}}\n')
print("wrote", len(outs), "answers; score them with the same grader as the BF16 run")
quant.note: Needs GPUs that support FP8 (Hopper-class or newer) for the FP8 model; the model id is an example of a published FP8 checkpoint. Compare against the BF16 model on your own evals.

specdec.scenario: A self-hosted model generates trade-confirmation summaries at 40 tokens per second with plain decoding. Drafted tokens rejected or discarded each step.

ast.title: Loading only the function node
ast.code:
src = open("billing.py", "rb").read()
tree = parser.parse(src)
fn = find_function(tree.root_node, "apply_tax")
snippet = src[fn.start_point[0]:fn.end_point[0]].decode()
context = [snippet] + [c.text.decode() for c in find_references("apply_tax")]
patch = llm_edit(issue, context)
new_src = src[:fn.start_byte] + patch.encode() + src[fn.end_byte:]
ast.explain: start_point and end_point are (row, column) pairs, so this slices the file by line numbers as if they were byte offsets: bytes 41 to 56 instead of lines 42 to 57. Slice the source with the node’s byte offsets.

also.5: Adding callers is the right context to include.
also.7: Splicing by start_byte and end_byte is correct: it replaces exactly the function’s bytes.

specdec.title: Verifying drafted tokens (greedy)
specdec.explain: At the first mismatch the target’s own token must replace the draft’s. Appending the rejected draft token changes the output, which breaks the guarantee that speculative decoding produces what the target model alone would.
specdec.fix: out.append(preds[i])   # the target’s token replaces the rejected draft

also.9: When every drafted token is accepted, the target’s next prediction comes free from the same pass. That bonus token is correct.

prefix.title: Building the prompt for every request
prefix.explain: Per-user text at the very start makes the first KV block different for every user, and because each block hash includes everything before it, none of the 6,000 shared tokens can be reused. Put the shared system prompt and tools first and per-user details after them. (This replaces lines 3–5.)
prefix.fix:
SYSTEM_PROMPT             # shared prefix first
        + TOOL_DEFINITIONS
        + f"User: {user.name} · Plan: {user.plan}\n"

also.6: History after the shared prefix is fine: each turn extends the previous prompt, so earlier turns stay cached.

disagg.title: Measuring the two phases
disagg.explain: Measuring from arrival folds queueing and prefill into TPOT, so requests with long prompts look like slow decoding. The rebalancer then moves GPUs away from prefill, which makes TTFT worse. TPOT runs from the first token to the last.
disagg.fix: tpot = [(r.done_at - r.first_token_at) / (r.out_tokens - 1) for r in reqs if r.out_tokens > 1]

also.2: TTFT from arrival to the first token is the right definition.
also.8: Adding decode capacity when TPOT breaches its target is the right response, once TPOT is measured correctly.

graphs.title: Earliest finish time of a step
graphs.explain: A step can start once its slowest prerequisite finishes, so the finish times of its dependencies combine with max, not sum. Summing gives 13 s for E, worse than running everything in sequence (11 s); the right answer is 6 s.
graphs.fix: return SECS[n] + max((finish(d) for d in DEPS[n]), default=0)

also.1: The dependency map is right: B, C and D need only A, and E needs all three.

latbudget.title: One timeout for all three tools
latbudget.explain: The timeout wraps the whole gather. When only the exchange log is slow, wait_for cancels all three calls, including order status and margin, which finished in under half a second, so the fallback has no facts at all. Put the timeout on the slow call alone, with a small capped() helper that returns a fallback value on timeout, so the fast results survive and only the exchange reason is missing.
latbudget.fix: status, margin, log = await asyncio.gather(order_status(order_id), margin_check(order_id), capped(exchange_log(order_id), 1.5))

also.4: Correct: the three calls are independent, so gathering them in parallel is right.
also.8: Correct in spirit: timeouts need a fallback, but it should carry the results that did arrive.

serving.title: Measuring serving throughput
serving.code:
lat, toks = [], 0
for p in prompts:                      # 200 real prompts
    t = time.perf_counter()
    r = client.chat.completions.create(model=M, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": p}], max_tokens=300)
    lat.append(time.perf_counter() - t); toks += r.usage.completion_tokens
print(toks / sum(lat), "tok/s")
serving.explain: Requests are sent one after another, so the server never batches. The test measures single-stream speed, not capacity, and makes the GPU look many times slower than it is.
serving.fix: results = await asyncio.gather(*(one(p) for p in prompts))   # concurrent requests

also.4: Capping answers at 300 tokens matches production, which is right.
also.6: Tokens ÷ time is the right measure once requests run concurrently.

calib = load_dataset("allenai/c4", "en", split="train[:512]")["text"]
model.quantize(calib, batch_size=4)          # GPTQ 4-bit

quant.fix: calib = [l.strip() for l in open("our_prompts_hi_en.txt", encoding="utf-8")][:512]

also.3: Quantising with the calibration set is the right step.
also.4: Saving the quantised model is fine.

2: The repo map has 4,100 symbols. How does the agent choose a file?
It reads every file in full first
The model ranks files from the map, using the issue text
The map is compact enough to fit in context; full files are not.

The exact span of Invoice.apply_tax: lines 42 to 57
A list of every line containing the word tax
A tree gives structure: the function node and its exact start and end.

Nothing: smaller is always better
Its callers, found with find-references
The fix changes behaviour that callers depend on, including one in another file.

The file is re-parsed to check for syntax errors
The tests are skipped because the edit is small
Re-parsing catches a broken edit instantly, before a slower test run.

Yes: it parses, so it works
Not until the tests pass
Valid syntax is not correct behaviour. Tests decide.

2: The draft proposed 4 tokens. How many target passes does checking them take?
One pass
Four passes, one per token
The target scores all drafted positions in parallel in a single forward pass.
3: “five” and “business” match the target’s predictions. What happens to them?
Both are accepted
They are re-generated by the target to be safe
Matching tokens are kept; that is where the speed-up comes from.
4: The target predicted “days” where the draft wrote “weeks”. What happens?
“weeks” is kept and marked uncertain
“days” is used and the rest of the draft is discarded
The first mismatch is replaced by the target’s own token, so the output matches the target model.
5: Which number decides whether speculation pays off?
The acceptance rate on your real prompts
The size of the target model
Low acceptance means paying for drafts that are thrown away.
6: k = 4, α = 0.7 gives 2.77 tokens per pass. With draft cost 0.05 per token, what is the speed-up?
About 2.8×
About 2.3×
The step costs 1 + 4 × 0.05 = 1.2 target passes, so 2.77 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 2.3×.

2: Why does each block’s hash include the hash of the block before it?
So a block matches only when everything before it matches too
To make hashing faster
KV values depend on all earlier tokens, so a block can be reused only if its whole prefix is identical.
3: The first request arrives with an empty cache. What happens?
It is rejected until the cache warms up
All tokens are prefilled and the blocks are kept
The first request pays the full cost and leaves its blocks for the next one.
4: Request B shares the 6,000-token prefix and adds 300 tokens. How many tokens are prefilled?
The 375 shared blocks are looked up; only the new 300 tokens are computed: 0.03 s.
5: Request C has a timestamp in the first line. How much can be reused?
Everything after the first line
Nothing
The first block differs, and every later block hash depends on it, so nothing matches.
6: GPU memory is full. Which cached blocks go first?
The least recently used
The longest prefixes
LRU eviction keeps hot prefixes, such as a shared system prompt, resident.

2: A 1.5 s prefill runs on a GPU that is also decoding at 30 ms per token. What do those streams see?
A pause of about 50 tokens
No change: prefill and decode run in parallel
1.5 s ÷ 0.03 s = 50 tokens of stall, which users see as a stutter.
3: Which kind of GPU work is prefill?
Memory-bandwidth-bound, like decode
Compute-bound
Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel; decode reads weights and KV cache for each single token.
4: Prefill is done on one GPU and decoding happens on another. What must move?
Only the prompt text
The prompt’s KV cache
The decode GPU needs the KV cache so it does not recompute the prompt; that is the transfer cost of splitting.
5: What happens to p95 TPOT once decode GPUs never run prefill?
It stays steady, around 35 ms
It rises, because fewer GPUs decode
With 6 decode GPUs each serves about 33 streams without interruptions, so TPOT is steady and within target.
6: TTFT breaches its target while TPOT has room. What do you change?
Move a GPU from decode to prefill
Move a GPU from prefill to decode
TTFT is set by the prefill pool, so it needs the extra capacity.

2: A has finished. Which steps are ready?
Only B, the next one in the list
B, C and D
Each of them depends only on A.
3: Why cap concurrency with a semaphore?
So a wide fan-out does not exceed rate limits
Because asyncio cannot run more than 3 tasks
Parallelism multiplies the request rate; a cap keeps it within what each API allows.
4: D times out on its first attempt. What should happen to B and C, which finished?
Keep their results and retry only D
Rerun them together with D
Checkpointed results are reused; only the failed node is retried.
5: When can E start?
When all of B, C and D have returned
As soon as the first of them returns
E is a join: it needs all three results.
6: Durations: A 1 s, B 3 s, C 2 s, D 4 s, E 1 s. How long does the graph take?
6 s
1 + max(3, 2, 4) + 1 = 6 s. The critical path is A → D → E.

2: The first trace shows tools 1,550 ms at p50 and 3,400 ms at p95. Which number should the budget be checked against?
The p95, 3,400 ms
The p50, 1,550 ms
The budget is written at p95; the slow tail is where users give up.
3: The answer call takes 2,400 ms and its first token arrives at 500 ms. With streaming, how much sooner do words appear?
1,900 ms sooner
No sooner: the call still takes 2,400 ms
Streaming shows words at the first token, 2,400 − 500 = 1,900 ms before the call ends.
4: Tools of 300, 450 and 800 ms run with gather. How long does the step take?
800 ms, the slowest
1,550 ms, the sum
Parallel calls take as long as the slowest one.
5: The exchange log’s p95 is 2,400 ms, and 8% of calls take over 1.5 s. What does a 1.5 s timeout do to that step’s p95?
Caps it at 1,500 ms, and 8% of answers fall back
Leaves it at 2,400 ms
More than 5% of calls hit the cap, so the p95 becomes the cap; the price is 8% degraded answers.
6: After merging the intent call, what is the p95 total? Tools 1,500, retrieval 200, answer 3,300 ms.
1,500 + 200 + 3,300 = 5,000 ms, inside the 5.5 s budget; the 900 ms intent p95 is gone.

2: A sequence finishes mid-batch. What happens to its slot?
A waiting request joins at the next step
It stays empty until the batch ends
That is continuous batching.
3: Lowering max context from 32k to 8k does what?
Frees KV memory for more sequences
Nothing
Less memory reserved per sequence.
4: 8 requests a second × 300 tokens needs?
2,400 tokens a second
300 tokens a second
5: One GPU at 80% busy gives p95 18 s. Two GPUs?
About 8 s
About 18 s
Headroom shortens the queue.
6: Two GPUs at ₹220 an hour, 8.64M tokens an hour. Cost per 1M?
About ₹51
About ₹440

2: FP8 weights for a 70B model take about?
70 GB
140 GB
One byte per parameter.
3: How many 80 GB GPUs does the FP8 model need?
Two
Four
70 GB plus KV cache.
4: What does an FP8 KV cache change?
More sequences fit, so throughput rises
Nothing
Half the cache memory.
5: Which evals should be re-run?
Your own Hindi and English legal set
Only a general benchmark
Your tasks and languages.
6: FP8 costs 0.5 points and halves GPUs. 4-bit?
One GPU but −1.5 points
No loss
The larger drop may matter.

specdec: The large model checks the drafts.
one forward pass for several tokens
one pass|single pass|forward pass|parallel|at once|in one
All drafted tokens are checked in a single pass.
accepting a prefix and correcting a mismatch
Accepted tokens are kept; the first mismatch is replaced.
The output matches what the target alone would produce.
The speed-up depends on the acceptance rate.
prefix: Attention keys and values for processed tokens.
The shared part skips prefill entirely.
It cuts time to first token.
Any change early in the prompt defeats it.
Hit rates depend on routing and GPU memory.
disagg: Inference has a prefill phase and a decode phase.
Prefill is compute-bound; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound.
They run on separate GPU pools.
The KV cache moves from prefill to decode workers.
Long prompts stop stalling other users’ streams.
Each pool is sized for its own latency target.
graphs: a graph of steps with dependencies

Results are joined before the next step.
the critical path sets the total

Nodes retry, time out and resume from checkpoints.

Every stage is traced and timed.
Status lines and streamed tokens show progress early.

ast: A stack trace points to line 812 of a 5,000-line ledger.py, inside post_entry(). What should the agent load first?
The post_entry function node and its callers
The last 100 lines of the file

(30 + 3 × 15) lines × 12 tokens = 75 × 12 = 900 tokens, against 48,000 for the whole file.

Whether a match is a definition, a call or a comment
The exact start and end of a function
Which class a method belongs to
The runtime value of a variable

A compact list of files with their classes and function signatures, not full bodies

Replace the node’s byte range rather than rewriting the file
Run the tests that cover the changed code

The draft model’s public benchmark score

Yes, if k is large enough
The first token waits for prefill. Speculation helps the tokens after it.
prefix: A self-hosted agent resends an 8,000-token system prompt and tool list on every step, and time to first token is 1.2 s. What is the first thing to try?
Prefix caching with a byte-stable prompt start
Most of the wait is prefill on the repeated prefix, which prefix caching skips.
A prompt is 8,000 shared tokens plus 400 new ones, and prefill runs at 20,000 tokens per second. What is the prefill time with a warm cache?
Only the 400 new tokens are prefilled: 400 ÷ 20,000 = 0.02 s, against 0.42 s without the cache.
Prefix caching is enabled, yet the hit rate is 0%. The system prompt starts with “Today is {date} {time}.” What is wrong?
The changing timestamp makes the first block differ, so nothing after it can match
Hit rate is always 0% at first
Move per-request text to the end of the prompt.
Which changes stop requests from reusing a shared cached prefix? Select all that apply.
A request ID in the first line
Tool definitions listed in a different order each time
Appending the user’s message at the end
Changing one word in the system prompt
Anything that changes early tokens breaks the match. Content appended at the end does not.
vLLM caches KV in 16-token blocks and only full blocks are reused. A shared prefix is 5,000 tokens. How many blocks can be reused?
5,000 ÷ 16 = 312.5, so 312 full blocks (4,992 tokens) are reusable.
Hit rate is 90% on a single replica but 30% across 8 replicas behind a round-robin load balancer. What is the fix?
Each replica has its own cache. Send requests that share a prefix to the replica that holds it.
How does prefix caching differ from a response cache?
It reuses attention state for a shared prompt start and still generates a fresh answer
A response cache skips the model entirely; prefix caching only skips repeated prefill work.
How does SGLang organize its cached prefixes?
A radix tree of token sequences (RadixAttention)
The radix tree finds the longest shared prefix, which suits branching agent workloads.
What is true about cached prefix blocks and GPU memory? Select all that apply.
Cached blocks use the same GPU memory as live requests
They can be evicted under memory pressure
Least recently used blocks usually go first
Caching raises the model’s maximum context length
Caching trades memory for recomputation; it does not change the context limit.
An advisory bot handles 10,000 requests a day, each with a 6,000-token shared prefix and 500 new tokens. With a 100% hit rate, how many prefill tokens are saved per day?
6,000 × 10,000 = 60,000,000 tokens that no longer need prefill.
In a multi-turn claims chat, each turn appends to the previous prompt. What can be reused on turn 5?
The system prompt and all earlier turns, as long as they are not rewritten
Each turn extends the cached prefix, so only the newest message needs prefill.
Does prefix caching change the model’s answers?
No: the reused keys and values are the ones prefill would have computed
It skips repeated work without changing what the model sees.
Which workloads benefit most from prefix caching? Select all that apply.
Agent loops that resend the same system prompt and tools each step
Many users sharing one set of instructions
Thousands of different long documents, each asked about once
Multi-turn chats that extend earlier turns
Reuse needs repetition. One-off documents share nothing to reuse.
A team calls a hosted model API rather than self-hosting. How do they get the benefit of prefix caching?
Use the provider’s prompt caching, for example cache_control breakpoints in Anthropic’s API or automatic caching in OpenAI’s
Hosted providers expose the same mechanism as prompt caching, with their own pricing and rules.
12 tenants, 4 replicas, and each replica can keep 3 tenants’ prefixes. With random routing, what hit rate would you expect?
Every replica sees all 12 tenants and holds 3: about 3 ÷ 12 = 25%. Cache-aware routing (3 tenants per replica) would reach 100%.
What should you monitor after enabling prefix caching? Select all that apply.
Time to first token at p50 and p95
Hit rate, TTFT and memory show whether caching works and what it costs.
Which practices keep the prompt prefix stable? Select all that apply.
Serialize tool schemas deterministically, for example with sorted keys
Put timestamps and request IDs at the end
Shuffle few-shot examples on every request
Shuffling examples changes early tokens on every request.
Storing the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like operating-system pages, so memory is used efficiently and blocks can be shared
A way to page through documents
Introduced with vLLM; block sharing is what makes prefix reuse cheap.
A tutoring app puts each student’s name and grade at the top of a 7,000-token system prompt. What should change?
Move the student details after the shared instructions
Shared content first, per-user content last.
Prefill runs at 12,000 tokens per second. Prompts are 9,000 shared + 600 new tokens, and 80% of requests hit the cache. What is the average prefill time?
disagg: What mainly limits the prefill phase?
All prompt tokens are processed in parallel, so prefill is compute-bound.
What mainly limits the decode phase?
Each new token requires reading the weights and KV cache, so decode is memory-bandwidth-bound.
A 20,000-token prompt takes 1.2 s to prefill on a GPU where streams decode at 40 ms per token. How many tokens could each waiting stream have produced during that prefill?
Which symptom most suggests disaggregated prefill would help?
p95 time per output token spikes whenever long documents are uploaded, while TTFT is fine
All requests are slow at night
Long prefills interfering with decode is exactly the problem it solves.
What does a disaggregated deployment need? Select all that apply.
A fast interconnect between prefill and decode GPUs
A way to transfer KV caches
A router that picks a prefill and a decode worker
Splitting phases adds transfer and routing; model size is unrelated.
A model has 32 layers, 8 KV heads and head dimension 128, stored in 16-bit precision. How much KV cache does one token need?
At 128 KiB per token, a 10,000-token prompt’s KV cache is about 1.31 GB. How long does it take to move over a 50 GB/s link?
In a split deployment, p95 TTFT misses its target while p95 TPOT has plenty of room. What do you change?
Add prefill capacity, for example by moving a GPU from decode
TTFT is set by the prefill pool.
Which are signs you do not need disaggregation yet? Select all that apply.
A small model on a single GPU
p95 TPOT spikes whenever long prompts arrive
Spikes caused by long prompts are the reason to consider it.
What is the core idea of DistServe?
Run prefill and decode on different GPUs and tune each for its own latency target
It optimizes goodput under separate TTFT and TPOT targets.
Which metrics should you track for a disaggregated service? Select all that apply.
Averages hide the per-phase behaviour you are tuning.
Which technique reduces decode stalls on a shared GPU without separate pools?
Chunked prefill: long prompts are processed in pieces interleaved with decode steps
Chunking bounds how long any decode step waits, at some cost to TTFT.
8 GPUs serve 200 streams with 2 prefill and 6 decode GPUs. If you move to 3 prefill GPUs, how many streams does each decode GPU serve?
200 ÷ 5 = 40 streams per decode GPU, so TPOT will rise a little.
What did Splitwise propose beyond splitting the phases?
Running each phase on hardware suited to it, such as different GPU types
Training a new model per phase
Decode needs less compute, so older or cheaper GPUs can serve it efficiently.
Mooncake, a KV-cache-centric disaggregated architecture, was built to serve which product?
Its paper describes serving Kimi with a disaggregated, KV-cache-centric design.
What are the downsides of disaggregated serving? Select all that apply.
More components to deploy and monitor
The prefill-to-decode ratio needs ongoing tuning
Outputs are identical; the costs are operational.
A response has 401 output tokens. The first token arrives at 2.0 s and the last at 14.0 s. What is its TPOT?
Why not simply add more GPUs to the shared pool instead of splitting it?
Each long prefill still interrupts every stream on the GPU it lands on; more GPUs only make it less frequent
Splitting needs fewer GPUs in every case
Interference is structural in a shared pool; splitting removes it.
Which projects support prefill–decode disaggregation? Select all that apply.
Prefill and decode nodes are joined by 10 Gb Ethernet, about 1.25 GB/s. A 3.9 GB KV cache must move for each long prompt. What should you conclude?
Transfer takes about 3.1 s, adding directly to TTFT: keep phases together or get a faster link
3.9 ÷ 1.25 ≈ 3.1 s of extra TTFT per long prompt outweighs the benefit.
graphs: A trip agent searches flights (3 s), hotels (4 s) and visa rules (2 s), which are independent, then builds the itinerary (1 s). How long does it take as a graph?
max(3, 4, 2) + 1 = 5 s, against 10 s in sequence.
What is the critical path of an agent workflow?
The longest chain of dependent steps, which sets the minimum total time
The step with the most tool calls
The step most likely to fail
Only shortening the critical path reduces total latency.
What should every node in an agent graph have? Select all that apply.
Explicit inputs, timeouts and retries make parallel execution safe and resumable.
After fanning out 50 product lookups at once, many fail with HTTP 429. What is the fix?
Cap concurrency, for example with a semaphore, and back off on 429s
Parallelism multiplies the request rate; respect the API’s limits.
A takes 2 s; B (5 s) and C (3 s) both need only A; D needs B and C and takes 1 s. Which change reduces total time?
Speed up nothing: it is already optimal
Total = 2 + max(5, 3) + 1 = 8 s. B is on the critical path; C is not.
In a parallel graph, the fraud-score step sometimes reads an empty account profile. What is the likely cause?
A hidden dependency: it needs the profile step’s output but the graph does not say so
Declare the dependency so the runtime orders the steps.
A 9-step claims workflow fails at step 7 and restarts from step 1 every time. What would help most?
Checkpoint finished steps so a retry resumes at step 7
Checkpoints turn a full rerun into a retry of the failed node.
Runs “decide” after all three nodes have finished
Runs the three nodes in sequence
A list of sources creates a join that waits for all of them.
Which are good candidates for parallel execution? Select all that apply.
Independent sub-questions of a research task
Two steps that update the same record
Steps that write the same state conflict; they need ordering.
An agent makes 5 independent API calls of 1.5 s each, then a 0.5 s summary. How long does it take with all calls in parallel?
Plans function calls as a dependency graph and executes independent ones in parallel
A planner produces a DAG of calls that an executor runs concurrently.
A model API returns three tool calls in one response (parallel tool use). What should the application do?
Execute them concurrently and return all results together
Ask the model to choose one
The model has signalled they are independent, so run them at the same time.
A prior-authorization workflow must wait up to three days for a doctor’s approval and survive deployments meanwhile. What fits best?
Durable execution with checkpoints, such as Temporal or a checkpointed LangGraph run
Long waits need state that survives restarts.
What are the risks of parallelizing an agent’s tool calls? Select all that apply.
Hitting rate limits all at once
The risks are real but manageable; parallelism does not guarantee errors.
Four independent bank API calls take 3 s each, and a semaphore allows 2 at a time. How long do they take?
Two waves of two calls: 2 × 3 = 6 s.
Tasks vary so much that no fixed graph fits them. What is a good approach?
Force one static graph on every task
Let a planner build a graph per task, then execute it
Dynamic planning keeps parallelism without a rigid structure.
One of three optional enrichment calls times out before the join. What should the join do?
Decide per join: for an optional input, continue with partial results and record the gap
Retry the whole workflow from the start
Required and optional inputs deserve different policies.
A workflow takes 11 s sequentially and 6 s as a graph. What is the speed-up?
Which help you decide what to optimize in an agent workflow? Select all that apply.
Trace spans with each node’s duration
The average duration of all nodes
A timeline (Gantt) view of the run
Averages hide which chain sets the total; traces and the critical path show it.
What should checkpointing let you do? Select all that apply.
Resume after a crash without rerunning finished nodes
Retry only the node that failed
Inspect the state at each step when debugging
Checkpoints store completed work and state; they are not a reason to skip checks.
latbudget: A trading app’s assistant averages 2.1 s per answer, but its p95 is 7.7 s and support tickets say it “hangs”. What should the latency budget be written against?
The p95 (or p99), per stage and end to end
The fastest answer of the day
Users who leave sit in the slow tail. Budgets are written and checked at p95 or p99, not the mean.
Stages in turn: intent 600 ms, tools 1,550 ms, retrieval 150 ms, answer 2,400 ms. With no streaming, when does the user see any text?
600 + 1,550 + 150 + 2,400 = 4,700 ms. Without streaming, the first visible text is the whole answer.
The answer call takes 2,400 ms and its first token arrives at 500 ms. Everything before it takes 2,300 ms. With streaming, when do the first words appear?
2,300 + 500 = 2,800 ms, 1,900 ms sooner than waiting for the full answer.
A recharge assistant calls three independent APIs taking 300, 450 and 800 ms. How long does that step take if they run in parallel?
Parallel calls take as long as the slowest: 800 ms, against 1,550 ms in turn.
Which changes shorten the real end-to-end time of an order-tracking assistant, not just how it feels? Select all that apply.
Running independent tool calls in parallel
Merging a separate intent call into the answer call
Showing a “Checking your order…” status line
Using a faster model for an early classification step
A status line improves perceived latency only; the other three remove waiting from the critical path.
A claims assistant shows a spinner for 5 s, then the whole answer. Which single change cuts abandonment most with the least work?
Streaming a status line and the answer tokens
Streaming shows progress within the first second and words as soon as the first token arrives, with no change to the pipeline.
An exchange-log API has a p50 of 800 ms and a p95 of 2,400 ms; 8% of calls exceed 1.5 s. With a 1.5 s timeout and fallback, what is that step’s p95 and the share of degraded answers?
More than 5% of calls hit the cap, so the p95 becomes 1,500 ms, and those 8% of answers are built without the log.
A team tightens a slow tool’s timeout from 1.5 s to 1 s. p95 improves by 500 ms, but degraded answers rise from 8% to 20% of 10,000 a day. How many more degraded answers is that each day?
20% − 8% = 12% of 10,000 = 1,200 more degraded answers a day.
Which belong in a latency budget for a patient-portal assistant? Select all that apply.
A p95 target for first visible words
A p95 target for the full answer
A maximum share of answers that may fall back
The GPU model used by the provider
The budget is written in user terms: first words, total time and how many answers may degrade. Hardware is not the user’s concern.
An NBFC’s loan assistant makes three LLM calls in a row: classify (700 ms), plan (1,200 ms) and answer (2,500 ms). Classify only picks one of five intents. What is the cheapest cut?
Replace classify with a small fast model or a rule, or fold it into the plan call
Run all three LLM calls in parallel
Add a cache in front of the answer call only
Use a bigger model for classify
An early step with a simple job can use a faster model or merge into the next call; the plan and answer depend on each other, so they cannot run in parallel.
Sequential stage p95s are 900, 3,400, 200 and 3,200 ms. Using the cautious rule of adding stage p95s, what is the end-to-end p95 estimate?
900 + 3,400 + 200 + 3,200 = 7,700 ms. Adding p95s overstates the true p95 slightly, which is the safe side for a budget.
Retrieval needs the rejection code returned by the exchange log. Can it run in parallel with the three tool calls?
Yes, always run everything in parallel
No, it depends on one tool’s output, so it must wait for it
Only if the model is streaming
Parallelism applies to independent calls. A step that needs another’s output stays after it on the critical path.
An assistant streams tokens. Which new problems must the team handle? Select all that apply.
Output guardrails must check text while it is still arriving
Errors can arrive after some text is already on screen
Clients must render partial text and a final state
Streaming does not slow the first token; it changes how checks, errors and rendering work.
Abandonment is modelled as 4% per second of blank screen after the first second. A UPI help bot shows nothing for 4.7 s. What share of users give up?
A trace shows p95 per stage: intent 900 ms, tools 1,500 ms, retrieval 200 ms, answer 3,200 ms. The budget is 5.5 s total at p95. Which change fits the budget without touching the tools?
Removing the separate intent call (merging it into the answer)

900 + 1,500 + 200 + 3,200 = 5,800 ms. Dropping the 900 ms hop and adding about 100 ms of prompt to the answer call gives 5,000 ms; faster retrieval saves too little, and streaming or a status line do not change the total.
Why does the tail matter more when an answer fans out to several tools?
Each extra dependency adds another chance to hit its slow tail, so the request’s p95 is set by the worst of them
Parallel calls are always slower than sequential ones
Tails cancel out across many calls
Fan-out only affects cost, not latency
The tail at scale: the more calls a request waits on, the more likely one of them is slow.
A lab-results assistant answers in 4 s. A status line “Fetching your report…” appears at 0.3 s. What has improved?
Perceived latency; the total is unchanged
A status line tells the user the system is working. Real latency still needs changes on the critical path.
A “why is my bill high?” assistant misses its budget. Which should you do first? Select all that apply.
Trace each LLM call, tool and retrieval and record p50 and p95
Find the stages on the critical path
Switch every stage to the smallest model available
Compare each stage’s p95 with its share of the budget
Measure before changing. Shrinking every model blindly can hurt quality without touching the stage that sets the total.
A courier API times out. What should the fallback answer do?
Invent a delivery date so the answer looks complete
Answer from the last known scan and say the live status is unavailable
A good fallback uses the data that did arrive and states what is missing, so users get facts rather than a confident guess.

Before: first words p95 7.7 s, total p95 7.7 s. After merging the intent call, parallel tools, streaming and a 1.5 s timeout: first words 2.6 s, total 5.0 s. By what percentage did the p95 total fall?
(7.7 − 5.0) ÷ 7.7 = 2.7 ÷ 7.7 ≈ 35%. First words fell further, by about 66%, because streaming also moved them earlier.
serving: Adds and removes requests at every decoding step
Runs one request at a time
8 requests a second × 300 tokens needs how many tokens a second?
Why does p95 rise sharply near full utilisation?
Requests queue as load nears capacity
GPUs slow down when hot only
Two GPUs at ₹220/h, 8.64M tokens an hour. Cost per 1M?
Which are serving engines with continuous batching? Select all that apply.
A load test sends requests one after another. Result?
A very long max context setting mainly costs?
KV memory, so fewer sequences fit
Static batching wastes GPU time because?
Batches wait for their longest answer
1 GPU, 60 tok/s one at a time; demand 600 tok/s. What happens?
Queue grows and requests time out
Why self-host instead of a hosted API? Select all that apply.
Data must stay in your own cloud
Steady high volume lowers cost per token
No one needs to run GPUs
Four GPUs at 20 req/s × 300 tokens with 3,000 tok/s each. Utilisation?
Which module-6 technique reuses a shared prompt prefix?
Engines implement it, but it is its own technique.
A GPU costs ₹220/h. Cost for a 30-day month running all day?
Low, spiky traffic of a few requests an hour usually favours?
What should a serving load test report? Select all that apply.
Headroom target for p95 is usually utilisation below about?
Throughput rises from 600 to 3,000 tok/s per GPU. Factor?
quant: BF16 uses how many bytes per parameter?
A 70B model in BF16 needs about how many GB of weights?
Which format usually loses least quality?
Which are 4-bit weight-only methods? Select all that apply.
What does an FP8 KV cache give?
Which models lose more quality at 4-bit?
Four GPUs at ₹300/h vs two. Hourly saving?
At large batch, weight-only INT4 can be?
What should be re-checked after quantising? Select all that apply.
Which format runs quantised models on laptops with llama.cpp?
₹300/h per GPU, 2 GPUs, 6.3M tokens an hour. Cost per 1M?
Which technique compresses embedding vectors rather than model weights?
FP8 needs which kind of GPU for full speed?
Recent GPUs with FP8 support (Hopper-class or newer)
Benefits of quantisation? Select all that apply.
A 70B FP8 model plus 20 GB KV on 80 GB GPUs using 72 GB each needs?
What is the first step before quantising?
Measure baseline quality, throughput and memory

ast.q: Why is a syntax tree better than grep for finding the code an agent must change?
pts: structure: definitions vs calls vs comments
ast.model: Grep matches text, so it returns comments, tests and similarly named strings, and cannot tell a definition from a call. A syntax tree knows structure: which node is the function, where it starts and ends, and which class it belongs to. Combined with find-references from a language server, the agent loads exactly the function and its callers, with far less noise and context.

ast.q: Design a localization pipeline for a coding agent in a large monorepo.
pts: hierarchical: file, then function, then lines
ast.model: Build a repo map of classes and function signatures with tree-sitter. Localize top-down: rank candidate files from the map, then functions within them, then line ranges. Load the chosen nodes plus their callers from find-references. After editing a node, re-parse the file and run the relevant tests before accepting the change.

ast.q: When can precise localization go wrong, and how do you guard against it?
pts: too narrow a view misses side effects
ast.model: Reflection, dependency injection and metaprogramming create call paths no static tree shows, and a view that is too narrow misses side effects in other files. Parsers can also lag new syntax. Guard with find-references plus a text search fallback, include callers, and rely on the test suite as the final check.

specdec.q: Explain why speculative decoding makes generation faster without changing the output.
pts: the target verifies them in one pass
decode is memory-bound, so extra positions are nearly free
acceptance rule keeps the target’s output
specdec.model: Decoding one token at a time leaves the GPU underused, because each step is limited by reading weights from memory. A cheap draft proposes several tokens and the target checks them all in one forward pass, which costs about the same as producing one. Accepted tokens are kept and the first mismatch is replaced by the target’s own token; with the standard acceptance rule the output distribution is exactly the target’s.

specdec.q: With α = 0.8 and k = 4, how many tokens does one target pass produce on average, and what else determines the real speed-up?
pts: divide by the cost of drafting
specdec.model: (1 − 0.8⁵) ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 0.672 ÷ 0.2 ≈ 3.36 tokens per pass.
