The real speed-up divides that by the cost of a step: one target pass plus k draft tokens, and at large batch sizes the extra verification is no longer free. Measure acceptance and tokens per second on your real prompts and traffic.

specdec.q: How would you pick a draft method for a code-editing assistant on a self-hosted model?
pts: prompt lookup or n-gram for edits that copy input
heads such as EAGLE or Medusa
specdec.model: Code edits copy much of the input, so start with prompt-lookup (n-gram) drafting, which needs no extra model. If acceptance is low, try a small draft from the same family with the same tokenizer, or EAGLE heads for the target. Tune the lookahead k on real edits by measuring acceptance and tokens per second.

prefix.q: Explain how prefix caching cuts time to first token for an agent.
pts: prefill skipped for the shared part
agents resend the same system prompt and tools
prefix.model: Before producing the first token, the server prefills the prompt, computing attention keys and values for every token. Agents resend the same system prompt, tool definitions and history on every step, so the KV cache for that identical prefix can be kept and reused. Only the new tokens are prefilled, which cuts time to first token and GPU work.

prefix.q: Your hit rate is high on one replica but low across eight. Diagnose and fix it.
prefix.model: Each replica keeps its own KV cache in GPU memory. With random routing every replica sees every tenant’s prefix, has room for only some, and evicts the rest, so hits fall. Route requests that share a prefix to the same replica, with session-sticky, consistent-hash or KV-aware routing, so each replica keeps a smaller set of prefixes warm.

prefix.q: How would you design prompts so they cache well?
pts: shared content first, per-user content last
no timestamps or IDs at the top
append history rather than rewriting it
prefix.model: Put stable content first: system instructions, then tool definitions, then long shared documents, and per-user or per-request content last. Keep that prefix byte-identical, so no timestamps, request IDs or reordered tool lists at the top. In multi-turn chats, append new turns instead of rewriting earlier ones, so each turn extends a cached prefix.

disagg.q: Why do prefill and decode compete badly on the same GPU?
disagg.model: Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and is limited by compute; decode produces one token per step and is limited by memory bandwidth. When a long prefill lands on a GPU that is also decoding, every stream there pauses, so improving time to first token for one user hurts time per output token for many others.

disagg.q: How would you decide whether to disaggregate an existing deployment?
pts: measure TTFT and TPOT separately at p95
long prompts and many streams competing
a fast interconnect for KV transfer
disagg.model: Measure p95 TTFT and TPOT separately under real load. Disaggregation pays off when long prompts and many concurrent streams interfere, so one or both targets are missed, and when a fast interconnect such as NVLink or RDMA can move KV caches quickly. At light load, or with only ordinary networking, the added components and transfer cost are not worth it.

disagg.q: A 30,000-token prompt’s KV cache is 3.9 GB. Compare the transfer time over RDMA at 50 GB/s and over 25 Gb Ethernet.
disagg.model: 3.9 GB ÷ 50 GB/s ≈ 79 ms over RDMA, but 25 Gb/s is about 3.1 GB/s, so Ethernet takes about 1.26 s. That time adds directly to time to first token, which is why disaggregated serving needs fast links; real systems also overlap transfer with computation, layer by layer.

graphs.q: Explain how an execution graph shortens an agent’s end-to-end time.
pts: total set by the critical path
graphs.model: The graph makes each step’s inputs explicit, so any steps whose inputs are ready run at the same time instead of one after another. Results are joined where a later step needs them. Total time falls from the sum of all steps to the length of the critical path, the longest chain of dependent steps.

graphs.q: A → (B 3 s, C 2 s, D 4 s) → E, with A and E taking 1 s each. What is the total, and which step would you optimize?
pts: speeding up B or C changes nothing
graphs.model: 1 + max(3, 2, 4) + 1 = 6 s, against 11 s in sequence. The critical path is A → D → E, so only making D faster, down to 3 s, where B takes over, reduces the total; speeding up B or C changes nothing.

graphs.q: What can go wrong when you parallelize an agent’s tool calls, and how do you prevent it?
pts: rate limits from a burst of calls
graphs.model: A step that silently needs another’s output will run on missing data, so declare every dependency. A wide fan-out can hit an API’s rate limit all at once, so cap concurrency and back off on 429 errors. Give each node a timeout and retry policy, and checkpoint finished nodes so a failure reruns only what failed.

latbudget.q: Explain how you would bring an LLM assistant inside a latency budget.
pts: p95 targets for first words and total
latbudget.model: Write the budget as p95 targets, such as first words within 3 s and the full answer within 5.5 s. Trace each LLM call, tool and retrieval and record p50 and p95 to find the critical path. Stream a status line at once and the answer tokens as they arrive; run independent calls in parallel; merge or shrink sequential LLM hops; and cap slow dependencies with timeouts and a planned, counted fallback.

latbudget.q: Intent call 600 / 900 ms, tools 300 + 450 + 800 ms in turn (p95 400 + 600 + 2,400), retrieval 150 / 200, answer 2,400 / 3,200 ms. What is the total at p50 and p95, and what does running the tools in parallel change? Show the working.
latbudget.model: In turn: 600 + 1,550 + 150 + 2,400 = 4,700 ms at p50 and 900 + 3,400 + 200 + 3,200 = 7,700 ms at p95. In parallel the tools take the slowest call: 800 ms at p50 and 2,400 ms at p95, giving 3,950 ms and 6,700 ms. Adding stage p95s is a cautious estimate; the exchange log’s tail still dominates, so it needs a timeout next.

latbudget.q: After a 1 s timeout on a slow tool, p95 latency looks excellent but complaints about vague answers rise. Diagnose it and say what you would change.
latbudget.model: A 1 s cap on a call with an 800 ms median cuts off a large share, here about 20%, so those answers are built without the tool’s data. Count degraded answers as part of the budget, loosen the timeout until the share is acceptable (1.5 s gives 8%), label fallback answers honestly, and look at hedged requests or caching for the slow dependency.

serving.q: How would you serve an open 8B model for a high-traffic support bot?
serving.model: Use a continuous-batching engine with paged KV memory such as vLLM or SGLang, load-test with real prompts at peak concurrency, keep utilisation below about 80% for the p95 target, and compare cost per million tokens with a hosted API.

serving.q: 2 GPUs at ₹220/h serve 2,400 tok/s. ₹ per 1M tokens?
A benchmark shows the GPU gives only 60 tokens a second. What would you check?
serving.model: Check whether requests were sent one at a time; single-stream speed is not capacity. Use a batching engine, test at realistic concurrency, tune memory and max context, and report throughput with p95.

quant.q: How would you cut the GPU cost of a self-hosted 70B model?
quant.model: Convert weights to FP8 to halve memory with little loss, add an FP8 KV cache for more concurrent sequences, consider 4-bit weight-only if it must fit on one GPU, and re-run your own evals per language and length before switching.

quant.q: 70B at 0.5 bytes per parameter plus 10% overhead. GB?
After 4-bit quantisation, Hindi answers got worse but English ones did not. Why, and what now?
quant.model: The calibration set was probably English only, and small or 4-bit models lose more on less-represented languages. Recalibrate on your own Hindi and English prompts, try FP8, and track evals per language.

procmem: Has the agent done this kind of task before?

cases.title: The research agent that takes twelve seconds
cases.brief: A stockbroking firm runs a market-research agent for its advisers on its own eight-GPU cluster with vLLM. An adviser asks something like “summarise today's move in HDFC Bank and what analysts are saying” and waits about 12.5 seconds. The business wants under six seconds before rolling it out to 2,000 advisers. Nobody has written the target down anywhere yet.
evidence: A trace of a typical query: five model calls, each spending 0.9 s on prefill of a 9,000-token prompt. vLLM prefix caching is enabled and its hit rate is 0% - the system prompt begins with the current date and time.
The agent calls four market-data tools one after another - quotes, news, fundamentals, broker notes - at about 1.5 s each. None of them needs another's output.
Answers are short, about 150 tokens, streaming at 45 tokens per second. Nobody complains about streaming speed. Load is around 30 concurrent users with no long document uploads.
About 40% of queries are the same morning routine, “brief me on my watchlist”, which the agent re-plans from scratch every day in seven steps.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.prefix: Start here. Five calls at 0.9 s of prefill is 4.5 seconds of the 12.5, and it is being paid for a reason stated in the evidence: the system prompt opens with the current date and time, so the cache that is already switched on can never hit. Move the volatile values to the end of the prompt and the prefix stops being recomputed - a configuration-free change with no quality risk and no new component to operate.
why.graphs: Four independent tools called in sequence is six seconds of waiting that could be about 1.5. Model the run as a graph so independent steps execute together, which turns a sum into a maximum. Watch the two pitfalls: hidden dependencies cause races, and four parallel calls can hit a market-data provider's rate limit all at once.
why.latbudget: Nobody has written the target down, and “under six seconds” needs to be a budget per stage before it can be engineered - prefill, tools, decode, with p95 rather than p50, since the slow 5% is where advisers give up. It also tells you where not to spend effort: the evidence already shows decode is not the problem.
why.procmem: Useful, and it comes from the memory module rather than this one: 40% of queries are the same morning routine re-planned from scratch in seven steps every day. Storing that routine as a procedure removes planning steps entirely, which is faster than making a plan quickly. Worth noting that the biggest remaining win may not be a performance technique at all.
why.serving: Useful as hygiene while you are in there: check that continuous batching is on and that max context is not set so high it reserves KV memory and shrinks the batch. At 30 concurrent users this is headroom for 2,000 advisers rather than today's bottleneck.
why.ast: Not needed: this is not a coding agent and there is no repository to localise within.
why.specdec: Not needed, and the evidence rules it out explicitly: answers are 150 tokens streaming at 45 tokens per second and nobody complains. Speculative decoding speeds up decode, which is roughly three seconds of a 12.5-second problem, and its gains shrink as the GPU gets busier.
why.disagg: Not needed: separating prefill and decode pays off in high-traffic serving with many concurrent streams, and this is 30 users. It would add KV transfer overhead and components to monitor for little benefit at this size.
why.quant: Not needed: the model already fits the eight-GPU cluster, and nothing here says GPU capacity is the constraint. The twelve seconds is prefill being recomputed and tools running in series.

firstWhy.graphs: The single largest slice - six seconds of serial tool calls that should be about 1.5 - and you will absolutely do it. It is second only because it needs care: hidden dependencies between those four tools would produce races, and four simultaneous calls may trip the data provider's rate limit, so it deserves thought, while the prefix fix is moving a timestamp.
firstWhy.latbudget: Correct that there is no written target and that one is needed before a 2,000-adviser rollout - and you should write it this week. As an ordering choice, a budget tells you where the seconds are, and this trace already does: 4.5 in prefill, 6 in serial tools, about 3 in decode.
firstWhy.serving: Worth checking and cheap. But at 30 concurrent users the serving engine is not what makes one query take 12.5 seconds - it is what will matter when there are 2,000 advisers instead of 30.

cases.model: Start with prefix caching, because 4.5 of the 12.5 seconds is prefill being recomputed on every one of five calls while the cache sits enabled and never hits - the system prompt opens with the current date and time, so move those to the end and keep the prefix byte-identical. Then turn the run into an execution graph so the four independent market-data tools go out together, converting roughly six seconds of serial waiting into about 1.5; check for hidden dependencies between them and for the provider's rate limit, which four simultaneous calls can trip. Write the latency budget down as part of this: a per-stage target measured at p95 rather than p50, because the slow 5% is where advisers abandon, and because it tells you not to spend effort on decode. Beyond this module, store the morning watchlist routine as a procedure rather than re-planning it in seven steps every day - 40% of queries would stop planning altogether. Check that continuous batching is on and max context is not reserving KV memory needlessly, as headroom for 2,000 advisers. Speculative decoding, disaggregated prefill and quantisation all target things this trace shows are not the problem, and there is no repository here to localise within.
cases.note: Every technique here was chosen or rejected from one trace, and the two largest wins were a prompt reordering and a dependency graph - neither of them a GPU change. Case 2's bottleneck is the serving engine and Case 3's is the GPU split, and in both the trace says so plainly.

prefix: Symptom 1 answers itself if you read the last sentence against the first: five calls, 0.9 s of prefill each, caching enabled, hit rate 0%, and a system prompt that begins with the current date and time. Why is a cache that is switched on never hitting?
The saving depends on the start of the prompt being identical between calls. Something at the very front changes every time, and that invalidates everything behind it.
Prefix Caching. The first pitfall - any change early in the prompt forcing a full recompute - is this symptom exactly.
graphs: Symptom 2: four market-data tools, 1.5 s each, called one after another, and the evidence says none of them needs another's output. What is being added up that should not be?

Describe the run as steps with declared dependencies instead of a sequence, and independent steps can go at once. Two warnings matter here: dependencies you did not notice, and what four simultaneous calls do to a provider.
Agent Execution Graphs. Read the pitfalls about hidden dependencies causing race conditions and parallel calls hitting rate limits together.
latbudget: The brief says the business wants under six seconds and that nobody has written the target down. Symptom 3 tells you nobody complains about streaming. What is missing before any of this can be engineered?
A number per stage, agreed and recorded - and measured at the percentile where users actually leave rather than the middle of the distribution.
Latency Budgets and Streaming. Note the pitfall about budgeting on p50 alone, and the one about a spinner with no status counting as solved.

drop.ast: AST-precise localisation finds exactly which lines of code need to change. What kind of agent is this?
drop.specdec: Speculative decoding makes tokens come out faster. Read symptom 3: how long are these answers, how fast do they stream, and who is complaining?
drop.disagg: Disaggregated prefill separates prefill and decode across GPUs for high-traffic serving with many concurrent streams. How many concurrent users does this system have?
drop.quant: Quantisation fits a big model on fewer GPUs and cuts cost per token. Which part of this 12.5 seconds is caused by GPU capacity?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right and you have the two big slices. Now split them by risk: one is moving a timestamp to the end of a string, and the other makes four calls fire simultaneously at a market-data provider.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Six seconds of serial tool calls is the largest single slice of the 12.5 and could become about 1.5.
4.5 seconds is spent recomputing a prefix the cache is already configured to hold, and the fix is reordering the prompt with no behavioural risk.
No latency target has been written down, and a 2,000-adviser rollout cannot be signed off without one.
whyFirst.why: Order by saving against risk when both are large. Parallelising the tools is the bigger win and it is your second step - but it changes execution order, can expose hidden dependencies, and may trip the data provider's rate limit, so it wants care. Moving a date out of the prompt prefix recovers 4.5 seconds and cannot break anything, because the cache is already enabled and waiting.

cases.title: The extraction service that blamed the GPU
cases.brief: An NBFC self-hosts a 70B-class model to extract fields from loan documents in Hindi, Tamil and English. It is spread across four GPUs because “it does not fit otherwise”. Someone benchmarked the setup, concluded the hardware was too slow, and asked for a bigger cluster. No latency target has ever been agreed, and the only number everyone accepts is that it feels slow.
evidence: The model runs at FP16 across four GPUs. FP8 has never been tried, and the workload is substantially Hindi and Tamil as well as English.
The benchmark that declared the GPU too slow sent one request at a time. Continuous batching is off, and max context is set to 128k, which reserves KV memory and holds the effective batch at three.
The cluster now runs at about 97% utilisation. p95 latency has gone from 4 s to 38 s while p50 has barely moved.
There is no written latency target. Priorities are set by whatever felt slow last week.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.serving: Start here, because the headline conclusion is wrong and the evidence says why. A benchmark that sends one request at a time measures a GPU doing nothing, which is the first pitfall of this technique word for word; continuous batching is off; and a 128k max context reserves KV memory that holds the batch at three. Turn batching on, set max context to what the documents actually need, and re-benchmark under concurrency before anyone buys hardware. Also stop running at 97% utilisation, which is why p95 exploded while p50 did not.
why.quant: A 70B model on four GPUs at FP16 is the case quantisation exists for, and FP8 has never been tried - but do it second and do it carefully, because the trap is in this very workload: calibrating on English web text for Hindi and Tamil documents is the named pitfall, and judging the result on a general benchmark rather than your own extraction tasks is the next one. Do not assume 4-bit is the answer either; at larger batch it can be slower than FP8.
why.latbudget: There is no target, so there is no way to say whether 38 s at p95 is a failure or whether 4 s was ever good enough - and priorities are being set by feel. Write a per-stage budget measured at p95, since p50 has barely moved while the experience collapsed. That gap between p50 and p95 is the whole story of symptom 3.
why.prefix: Useful: extraction prompts over a fixed field schema share a long prefix across documents, so caching it is free throughput. Secondary to getting the batch off three.
why.graphs: Useful if a document's fields are extracted by several independent calls, which could then run together. Nothing in the evidence says they are, so treat it as a question to ask rather than a fix.
why.ast: Not needed: there is no code and no repository here, only documents.
why.specdec: Not needed, and actively poor value here: extraction outputs are short field values, and speculative decoding's gains shrink at large batch sizes - which is exactly where you are trying to get to.
why.disagg: Not needed: splitting prefill and decode suits large, high-traffic deployments, and this is one internal workload whose measured problems are a disabled batch and a four-GPU FP16 footprint. It would add KV transfer overhead and more components to monitor.

firstWhy.quant: The right second step, and FP8 on a 70B model is a genuine structural win. But quantisation changes model output, and on a Hindi and Tamil workload the calibration pitfall is waiting - whereas turning on continuous batching and fixing a 128k max context changes throughput with no effect on what the model says. Take the free throughput first, then re-measure before touching numerics.
firstWhy.latbudget: Correct that nobody can prioritise without a target, and write it immediately - it is what stops “whatever felt slow last week”. As the first move, though, you would be setting a budget against a configuration that is measuring itself wrong: one-request-at-a-time numbers and a batch of three are not the system's real capability.
firstWhy.prefix: Real and worth having - a fixed field schema across documents is an ideal shared prefix. But cached blocks compete with live requests for GPU memory, and the memory here is already being eaten by a 128k context reservation. Fix the reservation first.

cases.model: Start with the serving engine, because the conclusion that the GPU is too slow came from a benchmark that sent one request at a time - the textbook way to measure a GPU doing nothing. Turn on continuous batching, reduce max context from 128k to what the documents actually require so KV memory stops holding the batch at three, and re-benchmark under realistic concurrency before anyone approves more hardware. Pull utilisation back from 97%, which is why p95 went to 38 s while p50 barely moved. Then quantise: FP8 on a 70B-class model is the obvious structural win, but calibrate on Hindi and Tamil documents rather than English web text, judge quality on your own extraction tasks rather than a general benchmark, and do not assume 4-bit beats FP8 at the batch sizes you are moving towards. Write the latency budget down as part of this work, measured at p95, so priorities stop being set by whatever felt slow last week. Then cache the shared prompt prefix across documents. Speculative decoding suits long outputs and small batches, which is the opposite of this; disaggregated prefill is for far larger deployments; and there is no code to localise.
cases.note: The first thing to fix here was a measurement, not a system: a benchmark that sends one request at a time will always say the GPU is slow, and it was about to buy a cluster. Check how the number was produced before optimising against it.

serving: Symptom 2 describes how the benchmark was run: one request at a time. Then it says continuous batching is off and max context is 128k, holding the effective batch at three. Before accepting “the GPU is too slow” - what was actually measured?
A GPU serving one request is mostly idle. The technique to read is about how many requests a GPU can serve at once, and about two settings that are currently preventing that.
Serving Engines and Continuous Batching. All three pitfalls are in symptoms 2 and 3: benchmarking one request at a time, running near 100% utilisation, and a long max context shrinking the batch.
quant: Symptom 1: a 70B-class model at FP16 across four GPUs because it does not fit otherwise, FP8 never tried, and a workload that is substantially Hindi and Tamil. What is the technique - and what is the specific trap in that last clause?
Fewer bits per weight, so a big model fits on fewer GPUs. The danger is in what you calibrate on and what you measure quality against.
Quantisation for Inference. Read the pitfall about calibrating on English web text for a Hindi and Tamil workload, and the one about general benchmarks instead of your tasks.
latbudget: Symptom 4: no written latency target, priorities set by whatever felt slow last week. And symptom 3: p95 from 4 s to 38 s while p50 barely moved. What is missing, and which number should it be written against?
An agreed figure per stage - and the gap between p50 and p95 here tells you which percentile matters, because the middle of the distribution did not notice what users did.
Latency Budgets and Streaming. The pitfall about budgeting on p50 alone is symptom 3 in one line.

drop.ast: AST-precise localisation identifies the exact lines of code to change. What is this service processing?
drop.specdec: Speculative decoding helps long outputs, and its gains shrink at large batch sizes. How long are extracted field values - and which direction is this system's batch size about to move?
drop.disagg: Disaggregated prefill separates prefill and decode for large deployments with many concurrent streams. Is this a large deployment, or one internal workload with two settings misconfigured?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right, and one of them is about to prevent a hardware purchase. Before deciding what to change, look at how the damning number was produced - and ask which of your fixes alters what the model outputs and which only alters throughput.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A 70B model at FP16 on four GPUs is the structural inefficiency, and FP8 has never even been tried.
The benchmark that condemned the hardware sent one request at a time, and two settings are holding the batch at three - so the system's real capability is unmeasured.
p95 has gone from 4 s to 38 s with no written target, so nobody can say what good looks like.
whyFirst.why: Order by what you know versus what you have assumed. Quantisation is the bigger structural change and your second step, and the missing target must be written this week. But a one-request-at-a-time benchmark with batching disabled and a 128k context reservation is not a measurement of this cluster - it is a measurement of a misconfiguration, and it is about to justify buying more of it.

cases.tag: Reading everything to change one line
cases.title: The coding agent that reads the repository to fix a typo
cases.brief: A platform team runs a coding agent over a large monorepo for 400 concurrent developer sessions. The serving engine is well configured - continuous batching on, max context sized to the workload - and the model fits its GPUs comfortably at the precision the team has validated for code. The complaints are that it is slow to start answering, slow to finish, and that it misses callers it should have changed.
evidence: To fix a bug from a stack trace, the agent greps and reads about 40 files - roughly 300,000 tokens - before it edits anything. It still misses callers in other modules and a reflection-based call path.
Outputs are long: full file rewrites of 600 to 2,000 tokens, which developers watch appear at about 18 tokens per second. Much of each output is copied verbatim from the input file.

400 concurrent sessions with long prompts share GPUs where prefill and decode run together. Targets exist for both time to first token and tokens per second, and utilisation swings as large prefills arrive.
Nobody has written down what “fast enough” means. The team optimises whatever was slow last week.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.ast: Start here, because one fix addresses both complaints at once. Reading 40 files and 300,000 tokens before editing is the prefill that makes everything slow, and it still misses callers - so the brute-force approach is failing on correctness as well as speed. Parse the code and work from the syntax tree: go from the stack trace to the exact definition, and from the definition to every caller, which is both a fraction of the tokens and a complete answer. Keep its limits in mind: reflection and metaprogramming hide call paths, which is exactly the caller it missed, so pair it with tests rather than trusting it alone.
why.specdec: Outputs of 600 to 2,000 tokens at 18 tokens per second is a developer watching a file being retyped, and the evidence names the ideal condition: much of each output is copied verbatim from the input. That is what prompt-lookup decoding exploits, with a very high acceptance rate on exactly this kind of edit. Watch the trade-offs - the draft model wants GPU memory, and gains shrink as batch sizes grow.
why.disagg: This is the one deployment in this module big enough to want it: 400 concurrent sessions, long prompts, and targets for both time to first token and tokens per second - which is precisely the conflict disaggregation resolves, since large prefills arriving on shared GPUs are what make decode stutter. Accept the costs honestly: KV transfer over the network, and more components to run and monitor.
why.prefix: Useful, and it compounds with the first step: repeated prompts over the same files share long prefixes, and multi-turn sessions extend the previous turn. Across 400 sessions on many replicas you will need cache-aware routing, or the hit rate falls away.
why.latbudget: Useful and overdue - two targets exist but no written budget, so effort goes wherever the last complaint was. Write it per stage at p95. It is not first only because this trace already says where the time goes.
why.graphs: Not needed: locating, editing and testing are genuinely dependent steps, so there is little to run in parallel. Reading 40 files faster in parallel would also be solving the wrong problem - the answer is to read three.
why.serving: Not needed: the brief says continuous batching is on and max context is sized to the workload. Worth noting because this is Case 2's first move, and here it is already done.
why.quant: Not needed: the model fits its GPUs at a precision the team has validated for code, and code generation is unusually sensitive to numeric degradation. Nothing here says capacity is the constraint.

firstWhy.specdec: The symptom developers feel most - watching a file retyped at 18 tokens per second - and the conditions for a large win are unusually good here, so you will do it. But it makes a long output arrive faster, while the first fix makes most of that output unnecessary and the prefill a fraction of its size. Shrink the work before speeding it up.
firstWhy.disagg: Correct, and this is genuinely the right scale for it - 400 concurrent sessions with long prompts and dual targets is the textbook case. It is also the most expensive and most operationally complex change on the page, and the thing making prefill enormous is that the agent reads 300,000 tokens it does not need. Remove the load, then re-measure before re-architecting the serving tier.
firstWhy.latbudget: Right that two targets without a written budget means effort follows complaints, and you should fix that now. But a budget identifies where the seconds go, and this trace has already identified it: 300,000 tokens of prefill before a single edit.

cases.model: Start with AST-precise localisation, because it answers the speed complaint and the correctness complaint together: reading 40 files and 300,000 tokens before editing is what makes prefill enormous, and it is still missing callers. Work from the syntax tree instead - stack trace to definition, definition to every caller - which cuts the tokens by an order of magnitude and gives a complete caller list, while remembering that reflection and metaprogramming hide call paths, so keep tests around it. Then add speculative decoding, specifically prompt-lookup style, because the evidence names the ideal condition: much of each 600-to-2,000-token output is copied verbatim from the input, so acceptance rates on these edits are high; budget the draft model's GPU memory and expect smaller gains as batch grows. Then disaggregate prefill from decode, which this deployment is genuinely large enough to justify - 400 concurrent sessions, long prompts and targets for both time to first token and tokens per second is exactly the conflict it resolves - accepting the KV transfer overhead and extra components. Cache prefixes with cache-aware routing across replicas, and write the latency budget down at p95. Execution graphs have little independent work to exploit, the serving engine is already configured, and the model fits at a precision validated for code.
cases.note: The serving engine was Case 2's first move and is already done here; disaggregation was dismissed in Case 1 and is right here. Same eight techniques, three different traces, three different answers - and in each case the best first move reduced the work rather than accelerating it.

ast: Symptom 1 contains two complaints in one sentence: 40 files and 300,000 tokens read before a single edit, and callers still missed. What single change would improve both?

Stop searching text and start using the structure of the code - from a stack trace to the exact definition, and from a definition to every place it is called. Note what kinds of code this still cannot see.
AST-Precise Localization. Read the pitfall about dynamic code hiding call paths - symptom 1's missed reflection-based caller is exactly that.
specdec: Symptom 2: outputs of 600 to 2,000 tokens at 18 tokens per second, and - this is the clue - much of each output is copied verbatim from the input file. What technique has a special case for exactly that?
A cheap drafter proposes tokens and the big model verifies them in bulk. When the output largely repeats the input, there is a variant that needs no draft model at all.
Speculative Decoding. Note the mention of prompt lookup for edits that copy large parts of the input, and the pitfalls about acceptance rate, draft memory and large batches.
disagg: Symptom 3: 400 concurrent sessions, long prompts, prefill and decode on the same GPUs, targets for both time to first token and tokens per second, and utilisation swinging as large prefills arrive. What are those two targets doing to each other?
The two phases have different appetites and are competing. There is an architecture that stops them sharing hardware - and it is only worth it at a certain scale, which this is.
Disaggregated Prefill. Read the pitfalls about KV transfer overhead and extra components, then weigh them against 400 concurrent sessions.

drop.graphs: Execution graphs run independent steps together. Locate, edit, test - how independent are those, and would reading 40 unnecessary files in parallel be the right fix?
drop.serving: Continuous batching and max-context sizing decide how many requests a GPU serves. What does the brief say about this team's serving configuration - and which case in this module began here?
drop.quant: Quantisation fits a model on fewer GPUs. Does the brief describe a capacity problem - and what does code generation do to the risk of numeric degradation?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right and they are the most expensive set in this module. Before committing to the serving re-architecture, ask which fix makes the prefill smaller rather than faster - and note that one of your choices also fixes the missed callers.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Reading 300,000 tokens before an edit is both why prefill is huge and why callers are missed, so one fix addresses speed and correctness.
Prefill and decode competing on shared GPUs is what breaks both latency targets at 400 concurrent sessions.
Developers watch 2,000-token rewrites appear at 18 tokens per second, which is the complaint they voice most often.
whyFirst.why: Order by what reduces the work rather than accelerating it. Disaggregation is the right architecture at this scale and decoding speed is what developers feel - but both are ways of serving an enormous prefill faster, and that prefill is 40 files the agent did not need to read. Localise precisely and you cut the tokens by an order of magnitude, fix the missed callers, and get an honest baseline to re-measure the serving tier against.

quiz: Time to first token is 4 s on a self-hosted model, and every prompt starts with the same 7k-token system prompt. First fix?
Most of the wait is prefill on the shared prefix. Reusing its KV cache skips that work.
Tokens stream slowly (15 per second) on long answers, while time to first token is fine. What helps most?
The bottleneck is decoding. A draft model proposing several tokens per target pass speeds it up.
An agent calls three independent APIs one after another, 2 s each, then summarizes for 1 s. With an execution graph, what's the total?
The three calls run in parallel (2 s), then the summary (1 s).
A coding agent reads whole 3,000-line files to fix one function. What's the fix?
Navigate the syntax tree and load only the relevant nodes.
Every week the agent rediscovers how to add an API endpoint. What's the fix?
Procedural memory: save the workflow as a skill
Store the proven procedure once and reuse it.
On a shared GPU fleet, long 30k-token prompts make other users' token streams stutter. What's the fix?
Separate prefill and decode pools so long prompt processing never blocks decoding.
Speculative decoding gives almost no speed-up. Most likely cause?
The target model is too small
A low acceptance rate from a poorly matched draft
If the target rejects most drafted tokens, you pay for drafting without saving passes.
Prefix-cache hit rate is high on one replica but low across eight. Why?
The cache is per-replica and requests aren't routed to the replica holding their prefix
The cache is disabled on seven replicas
Use cache-aware or session-sticky routing so repeated prefixes land where their KV cache lives.
Which metric does prefill mainly determine?
Prefill processes the prompt before the first token appears; decode sets the pace after that.
Parallel tool calls started failing with HTTP 429 errors. Why?
The fan-out hits rate limits all at once
Cap concurrency per API and add backoff; parallelism multiplies request rate.

ast.t: A file has 3,000 lines at about 10 tokens each. The target function is 16 lines, and its two callers are 20 lines each. How many tokens does AST localization load?
ast.a: (16 + 20 + 20) lines × 10 = 560 tokens, against 30,000 for the whole file: about 50× less context.
iv: Why isn't grep enough for code localization?

Grep finds strings, not structure: it can't tell a definition from a call or a comment, misses renamed imports, and returns noisy matches. Syntax trees and language servers resolve symbols, scopes and references precisely.
What is a repo map?
A compact summary of a repository: files with their classes, functions and signatures (not bodies), often ranked by relevance, so the model can decide where to look without reading whole files.
mis: Sending whole files to the model
Send the relevant nodes plus immediate context
Editing text without re-parsing
Re-parse after every edit and run the tests

specdec.t: Lookahead k = 4. On average 3 drafted tokens are accepted per step, plus 1 token from the target. A target pass costs 1 unit and the draft costs 0.1 per token. Tokens per unit of cost?
specdec.a: Plain decoding: 1 token per unit. Speculative: 4 tokens per (1 + 4 × 0.1) = 1.4 units ≈ 2.86 tokens per unit, about 2.9× faster.
iv: Why doesn't speculative decoding change the output?

The target model checks every drafted token, and the acceptance rule keeps the output distribution identical to the target's own. Rejected tokens are replaced by the target's choice, so only speed changes.
When does speculative decoding help least?
When acceptance is low (a mismatched draft, creative high-temperature sampling), at large batch sizes where the GPU is already busy, or when the draft adds significant memory pressure.
mis: A draft model with a different tokenizer
Pick a draft from the same model family
Setting lookahead k very high
Tune k on real prompts by acceptance rate

prefix.t: A prompt is 6,000 shared tokens plus 300 user tokens, and prefill runs at 10,000 tokens per second. With prefix caching, how long does prefill take, in seconds?
prefix.a: Without caching: 6,300 ÷ 10,000 = 0.63 s. With the shared 6,000 reused: 300 ÷ 10,000 = 0.03 s before the first token.
iv: How is prefix caching different from a response cache?
Prefix caching reuses the attention KV state for shared prompt beginnings, and the model still generates a fresh answer. A response cache returns a stored answer and skips the model.
How do you keep prefix-cache hit rates high across many replicas?
Keep prompt prefixes identical, and route requests sharing a prefix (same session, tenant or system prompt) to the same replica with cache-aware or consistent-hash routing.
mis: Per-user text at the start of the prompt
Shared content first, per-user content last
Random load balancing across replicas
Cache-aware or session-sticky routing

disagg.t: Prefill of a 30k-token prompt takes 1.5 s. Decode produces a token every 30 ms. On a shared GPU, how many tokens could each waiting stream have produced during one prefill?
disagg.a: 1.5 s ÷ 0.03 s = 50 tokens of stall per stream, which users see as a stutter. Separate pools remove it.
iv: Why are prefill and decode bottlenecked differently?

Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel, so it's limited by compute. Decode produces one token per step and must read the model weights and KV cache each time, so it's limited by memory bandwidth.
What does disaggregation cost you?
Moving the KV cache between GPUs adds network traffic and latency, needs fast interconnects, and adds components to deploy, route and monitor. It pays off at high traffic with long prompts.
mis: Tracking only average latency
Track time to first token and time per output token separately, at p95
Disaggregating a small, lightly loaded service
Use it when long prompts and many streams compete

graphs.t: A takes 1 s, then B (3 s), C (2 s) and D (4 s) can run in parallel, then E takes 1 s. What's the total time with an execution graph, in seconds?
graphs.a: Sequential: 1 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 11 s. Graph: 1 + max(3, 2, 4) + 1 = 6 s. D is on the critical path, so speeding up B or C changes nothing.
iv: What is the critical path in an agent workflow?
The longest chain of dependent steps. It sets the minimum end-to-end time, so speeding up steps off the critical path doesn't reduce total latency.
How do you handle a failed branch in a parallel graph?
Give each node its own timeout and retry policy, checkpoint completed nodes so retries don't rerun them, and decide per join whether to continue with partial results or fail.
mis: Parallelizing steps that share state
Make dependencies explicit and merge results with reducers
Unlimited parallel fan-out
Cap concurrency to respect rate limits

latbudget.t: An assistant makes a 600 ms intent call, then three independent tool calls of 300, 450 and 800 ms, then a 150 ms retrieval, then a streamed answer call whose first token arrives 500 ms after it starts. If the tools run in parallel, when do the first answer words appear, in milliseconds?
latbudget.a: 600 + max(300, 450, 800) + 150 + 500 = 600 + 800 + 150 + 500 = 2,050 ms. With the tools in turn it would be 600 + 1,550 + 150 + 500 = 2,800 ms, and without streaming the user would wait for the whole answer.
iv: How would you set and enforce a latency budget for an LLM feature?

Agree targets with the product owner at p95, for example first words within 3 s and the full answer within 5.5 s. Trace every stage (each LLM call, tool and retrieval) and record p50 and p95. Find the critical path, then remove waits: stream early, run independent calls in parallel, merge or shrink LLM hops, and cap slow dependencies with timeouts and planned fallbacks. Alert when a stage’s p95 drifts past its share of the budget.
Streaming made users happier but the total time did not change. Was it worth it?

Yes, within limits. Perceived latency depends mostly on when something useful appears; a status line and streamed words cut abandonment even at the same total. But the total still matters for users who need the whole answer, and streaming cannot hide a 7 s p95. Treat streaming as the first fix, not the only one.
mis: Budgeting on the average response time
Set p95 targets per stage and end to end; the slow tail is where users leave
Adding a tight timeout and not counting fallbacks
Track the share of degraded answers and budget it like latency

serving.t: Two GPUs at ₹220 an hour each serve 2,400 output tokens a second. What is the cost per million output tokens in ₹?
serving.a: Tokens an hour: 2,400 × 3,600 = 86,40,000 = 8.64 million. Cost an hour: ₹440. ₹440 ÷ 8.64 ≈ ₹50.9 per million tokens.
iv: What is continuous batching?
The server adds new requests to the running batch at every decoding step and removes finished ones, instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish. GPUs stay busy, so throughput rises several-fold.
Why does p95 latency jump near full utilisation?
As load approaches capacity, requests queue; waiting time grows sharply above about 80% busy. Size capacity so peak load leaves headroom.
mis: Load-testing one request at a time
Test at realistic concurrency
Running GPUs near 100% busy
Keep headroom for the p95 target

quant.t: A 70B-parameter model in 4-bit weights uses 0.5 bytes per parameter plus 10% overhead for scales. How many GB of weights?
quant.a: 70 × 10⁹ × 0.5 = 35 GB; plus 10% = 38.5 GB, which fits on one 80 GB GPU with room for the KV cache.
iv: FP8 or INT4 for serving a 70B model?

FP8 first on GPUs that support it: half the memory with a very small quality change and good throughput at large batch. INT4 weight-only when you must fit on fewer GPUs or run small batches, after checking the larger quality loss on your tasks.
What does KV-cache quantisation buy you?
The cache for each sequence takes half the memory in FP8, so more sequences fit at once and throughput rises, at a very small quality cost.
mis: Calibrating on generic English text
Use prompts from your own traffic and languages
Trusting a general benchmark
Re-run your own evals before and after

gloss: KV cache
Stored attention keys and values for processed tokens, so they aren't recomputed.
prefill
Processing the whole prompt before the first output token; limited by compute.
decode
Generating output one token at a time; limited by memory bandwidth.
TTFT
Time to first token: how long until the first output token appears.
TPOT
Time per output token after the first; sets streaming speed.
draft model
A small, fast model that proposes tokens for a larger model to verify.
acceptance rate
Share of drafted tokens the target model accepts in speculative decoding.
AST
Abstract syntax tree: the structured parse of source code.
repo map
A compact list of a repository's files, classes and function signatures.
LSP
Language Server Protocol: editor tooling for definitions, references and symbols.
DAG
Directed acyclic graph: steps with one-way dependencies and no cycles.
critical path
The longest chain of dependent steps; it sets total latency.
procedural memory
Stored know-how, such as workflows and skills, that an agent can reuse.
latency budget
A written target for how long a user-facing request may take, usually at p95, split into shares for each stage.
perceived latency
How long a wait feels to the user; early status lines and streamed words shorten it even when total time is unchanged.
LLM hop
One sequential model call on the path to an answer; each adds its own time to first token and generation time.
continuous batching
Adding and removing requests from the running batch at every decoding step.
PagedAttention
Storing the KV cache in fixed-size pages so memory is not wasted and more sequences fit.
KV cache
Stored attention keys and values for tokens already processed, reused at each new step.
FP8
An 8-bit floating-point format for weights and activations, supported on recent GPUs.
AWQ
Activation-aware weight quantisation: a 4-bit weight-only method that protects the most important weights.
calibration set
Representative prompts used to set quantisation scales.

prefix.name: Prompt Caching
prefix.note: Same idea at two levels: prompt caching is what the API provider offers; prefix caching is the KV-cache reuse inside the inference engine.

prefix.name: Context Budgeting
prefix.note: Put stable content first so it can be cached, and the question last so it is used best.

prefix.name: Serving Engines and Continuous Batching
prefix.note: Serving engines implement prefix caching; shared prompts raise throughput further.

graphs.name: Process-Level Eval
graphs.note: Execution graphs make the trajectory explicit, which makes step-level scoring easier.

graphs.name: Action Policies and Approval Thresholds
graphs.note: Every tool node in an execution graph should pass the zero-trust policy gate.

graphs.name: Plan-and-Execute
graphs.note: A plan with independent steps becomes an execution graph whose branches can run in parallel.

graphs.name: Parallel and Sequential Tool Calls
graphs.note: An execution graph plans the whole workflow; parallel tool calls are the per-turn choice of which calls run together.

graphs.name: Retries, Timeouts and Idempotency
graphs.note: Graph nodes that replay after a crash need idempotent side effects.

graphs.name: Agent-to-Agent Protocols (A2A)
graphs.note: Graphs coordinate agents you own; A2A hands a task to an agent you do not.

graphs.name: Single vs Multi-Agent
graphs.note: Execution graphs run independent steps in parallel inside one agent; whenmulti asks whether those branches need separate agents, each with its own context and token bill.

graphs.name: Supervisor and Workers
graphs.note: In an execution graph the steps are fixed in advance; a supervisor decides them at run time.

graphs.name: Latency Budgets and Streaming
graphs.note: An execution graph is how the budget's parallel step is built: independent tool calls fan out and the critical path sets the total, which the budget then checks at p95.

ast.name: Context Pruning
ast.note: Loading only the needed code nodes is context pruning for coding agents.

specdec.name: Model Routing and Tiering
specdec.note: Both pair a small model with a large one: routing picks one per request, speculative decoding uses both on every step.

specdec.name: Serving Engines and Continuous Batching
specdec.note: Speculative decoding runs inside the same engines to cut per-token latency.

latbudget.name: Agent Execution Graphs
latbudget.note: An execution graph is how the budget's parallel step is built: independent tool calls fan out and the critical path sets the total, which the budget then checks at p95.

latbudget.name: Timeouts, Circuit Breakers and Fallbacks
latbudget.note: The timeout-and-fallback lever is a resilience pattern; the budget adds how tight the timeout may be and how many degraded answers are acceptable.

latbudget.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI Tracing
latbudget.note: Per-stage p50 and p95 come from traces: a span for each LLM call, tool and retrieval shows where the seconds go.

latbudget.name: Model Routing and Tiering
latbudget.note: Using a faster model for early steps is model routing applied to latency: a small model classifies, the large one answers.

serving.name: Prefix Caching
serving.note: Serving engines implement prefix caching; shared prompts raise throughput further.

serving.name: Speculative Decoding
serving.note: Speculative decoding runs inside the same engines to cut per-token latency.

serving.name: Distillation into a Small Model
serving.note: A distilled small model is usually self-hosted on one of these engines.

serving.name: Quantisation for Inference (FP8, INT4, KV Cache)
serving.note: Quantised models are served on the same engines; fewer GPUs and more sequences per GPU compound.

quant.name: Serving Engines and Continuous Batching
quant.note: Quantised models are served on the same engines; fewer GPUs and more sequences per GPU compound.

quant.name: Vector Compression (Scalar, Product and Binary Quantisation)
quant.note: Vector compression quantises embeddings; this quantises model weights and the KV cache.

quant.name: Evaluate Before and After Tuning
quant.note: Quantisation changes a model, so run the same before-and-after evals as for fine-tuning.

gifs.ast: The agent walks the syntax tree from billing.py to Invoice.apply_tax (lines 42 to 57), adds both callers with find-references, and loads 56 lines, 560 tokens, instead of 30,000 tokens for the whole file.
gifs.disagg: On a shared GPU a 1.5 s upload prefill stalls every token stream; with separate prefill and decode pools the KV cache moves in 79 ms and p95 time per token falls from 61 ms to 35 ms, meeting both targets.
gifs.graphs: A loan-underwriting workflow drawn as a graph runs the credit, bank-statement and employment checks in parallel, so total time equals the critical path A, D, E: 6 s instead of 11 s sequentially.
gifs.latbudget: Animated scene for Latency Budgets and Streaming at Tejas Trade, a fictional stockbroking app, answering “Why did it fail?” about a rejected order. On the left, six stage bars build up one after another on a 0 to 5 second axis: an intent call, order status, margin check and exchange log tool calls in turn, a help search and a 2.4-second answer call, finishing at 4.7 seconds. On the right, a phone shows the user’s question and a waiting spinner, labelled blank until 4.7 seconds. Next the intent bar fades away, the three tool bars slide to start together at zero, the help search and answer call move earlier, and the run now ends at 3.45 seconds; a dashed line marks a 1.5-second timeout on the exchange log, with 8% of answers falling back. Finally dashed markers show a status line at 0.3 seconds and the first answer words at 1.55 seconds, the phone shows “Checking your order…” and then the streamed answer “Rejected by the RMS: margin short by ₹1,840. Add funds, then place the order again.”, and a note reads p95 total 7.7 to 5.0 seconds, first words 2.6 seconds.
gifs.prefix: Three requests share a 6,000-token prompt prefix: the first prefills it and keeps the KV cache, the next two reuse it, so prefill falls from 18,950 to 6,950 tokens and time to first token for B from 0.625 s to 0.025 s.
gifs.quant: Bars show a 70B model's weights: 140 GB in BF16, 70 GB in FP8 and 38 GB in 4-bit, needing four, two and one 80 GB GPUs. On the service's own evals, quality is 86.0 for BF16, 85.5 for FP8 and 84.5 for 4-bit. FP8 weights with an FP8 KV cache cut the GPUs from four to two and the cost from ₹208 to ₹95 per million tokens.
gifs.serving: Two panels compare batching. With a static batch, four requests of different lengths run together, and shorter ones leave idle amber slots until the longest finishes. With continuous batching, new green requests fill each slot as soon as one finishes. A paged KV cache lets up to 128 sequences share each GPU step. At 8 requests a second, one GPU runs 80 percent busy with a p95 of 18 seconds and two GPUs give 8 seconds. Throughput rises from 600 to 3,000 tokens a second per GPU, about ₹51 per million tokens.
gifs.specdec: A draft model proposes four tokens, the target model keeps two, replaces the third and discards the fourth in one pass; at acceptance rate 0.60 and k = 4 this averages 2.31 tokens per pass, a 1.92x speed-up.

header.lede: Agents feel slow for three reasons: they take too many steps, each model call waits on prefill and token-by-token decoding, and tool calls run one after another. These techniques attack all three, from the agent’s code down to the inference server. Reusing proven routines is covered in the Memory & Context module.
